a15_0612539.speaker: Scott
a15_0612539.text: Rog. And we've got you. With everything looking ship-shape down here, what do you think about proceeding with the chlorination?

a15_0612539.speaker: Henize
a15_0612539.text: Okay, Dave. Go ahead.

a15_0612539.speaker: Scott
a15_0612539.text: All righty.

a15_0612539.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0612539.text: This is Apollo Control at 61 hours, 41 minutes. That in-flight repair of the chlorination port on the water tank was accomplished with 2 tools in the onboard toolkit. Tool 3 that you heard reference to is a hexagonal Allen wrench. Tool W is a ratchet that fits on to provide leverage for the wrench.

a15_0614506.speaker: Henize
a15_0614506.text: 15, this is Houston. Is Jim doing some exercising now? We're doing a little medical detective work down here.

a15_0614506.speaker: Scott
a15_0614506.text: Why, yes, as a matter of fact, he is. He's trying to get one of the compartments open.

a15_0614803.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0614803.text: This is Apollo Control at 61 hours, 54 minutes. Apollo 15 now 187,163 nautical miles [346,625 km] from Earth. Velocity; 2,995 feet per second [913 m/s].

a15_0614803.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0614803.text: This is Apollo Control at 62 hours, 4 minutes. Apollo 15 is 187,464 nautical miles [347,183 km] from Earth. Velocity; 2,990 feet per second [911 m/s]. To recap the water tank problem: at 61 hours, 15 minutes, Dave Scott reported a leak in the chlorination port of the water tank, just as he was getting ready to chlorinate the water for the evening. He reported it was a pretty good leak. Water was balling up around the port fairly rapidly. We had the crew close some pressure regulators to relieve the pressure inside the tank to slow the leak, then passed up a procedure involving the use of two o

a15_0621434.speaker: Scott
a15_0621434.text: Okay; we've got the presleep checklist if you're ready to copy. [Pause.]

a15_0621434.speaker: Scott
a15_0621434.text: Okay; crew status is good. No medication today. Onboard read-outs: Bat C, 37.0 [volts]; Pyro Bat A, 37.2; B, 37.2; RCS A, 89 [per cent remaining]; B, 86; C, 89; and D, 86. And the H 2 fans have been cycled, and the potable water has been chlorinated, and the vents and switches are all set. The cabin's [pressure] at 5.7 [psia, 39.3 kPa], and I'll give you an E-memory dump any time you're ready.

a15_0621434.speaker: Henize
a15_0621434.text: We copy; and stand by on memory dump.

a15_0621434.speaker: Scott
a15_0621434.text: Okay. You might be interested in another little item. All the meals have been consumed on schedule, and the - the pantry's even had a pretty rigid test so far.

a15_0621434.speaker: Scott
a15_0621434.text: And our trusty LMP came up with an interesting analogy relative to the last event. He wondered if the original Endeavour had ever sprung a leak like that.

a15_0621434.speaker: Henize
a15_0621434.text: Hey; that's a good question. We'll get our historians out to check that one. [Pause.] Hey, what did you do with all that extra water? Stick it overboard, or drink it, or what?

a15_0621434.speaker: Scott
a15_0621434.text: Oh, no; we've got a bunch of towels hanging up in the tunnel right now. Looks like somebody's laundry. [Pause.]

a15_0621434.speaker: Henize
a15_0621434.text: Sy [Liebergot]'s down here guessing that you hosed some of it overboard.

a15_0621434.speaker: Scott
a15_0621434.text: Well, you probably saw the motion of the spacecraft. We were just in that process when you came up with a procedure.

a15_0621434.speaker: Henize
a15_0621434.text: [Laughter.] Okay; fine. The PTC's still looking great.

a15_0621434.speaker: Henize
a15_0621434.text: Okay, Dave. We're ready for the E-mod dump.

a15_0622035.speaker: Henize
a15_0622035.text: 15, Houston. We finished the E-memory dump. The Surgeon - the Surgeon says that it's - it's your turn in that biomed harness. And, otherwise, we - don't have any - anything more down here. And, we're ready to secure - the - the voice communications any time you like.

a15_0622035.speaker: Scott
a15_0622035.text: Okay; very well. By the way, how are the biomed harnesses working out for the Surgeons? [Pause.]

a15_0622035.speaker: Henize
a15_0622035.text: The word is that we're getting good clean data, and they're very happy with it.

a15_0622035.speaker: Scott
a15_0622035.text: Okay; very well. See you in the morning.

a15_0622035.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0622035.text: This is Apollo Control at 62 hours, 21 minutes. We have secured voice communications with Apollo 15, now. [We] do not expect any more air/ground conversation tonight. Apollo 15 now 187,962 nautical miles [348,105 km] from Earth. Velocity; 2,981 [fps, 909 m/s]. We'll take the air/ground line down now. If there are any more conversations, we'll come back up. At 62 hours, 22 minutes; this is Mission Control, Houston.

a15_0622035.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0622035.text: This Apollo Control at 63 hours, 8 minutes. Flight Director Glynn Lunney and his team of flight controllers are preparing to relieve the Maroon team headed by Flight Director Milton Windler. There will be no change of shift briefing following this shift change. The next change of shift briefing is estimated for 7:15 am Central Daylight Time. We'll summarize the activities during this past 8 hours that the Maroon team has been on duty. [The] spacecraft was taken out of the Passive Thermal Control mode shortly after this team came on duty and Command Module Pilot Al Worden completed a series of

a15_0622035.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0622035.text: We said goodnight to the crew and secured communications at 62 hours, 21 minutes, shortly after Dave Scott reported that the crew status was good, they have taken no medication, that they've consumed all their meals on schedule, and that the cabin pressure was reading 5.7 pounds per square inch for the evening. He also gave readouts on - for batteries and the Reaction Control System quantities, all of which are good. We have, from the Flight Dynamics Officer [FIDO] on the Maroon team, Bill Boone, some updates on estimated - on predicted numbers during the next few maneuvers. This time, it appe

a15_0622035.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0622035.text: This is Apollo Control at 64 hours. We said goodnight to the crew about an hour and 40 minutes ago. The Flight Surgeon reported just a few minutes ago that it appears Dave Scott has now settled down and is asleep. Scott is the only crewman on whom we'll have biomedical data during the rest period. Just a few minutes ago, we passed into the lunar sphere of influence, a point at which for computational purposes, we begin computing the spacecraft's position with respect to the Moon rather than with respect to the Earth. And it's also the point at which the Moon's gravity becomes the dominant forc

a15_0700000.speaker: Parker
a15_0700000.text: Roger. Good morning, Dave. It's time to rise and shine.

a15_0700000.speaker: Parker
a15_0700000.text: And we've got the usual quota of checklist changes, Flight Plan updates, et cetera. When you guys are ready, give me a call. Looks like you guys had a good night's sleep last night, for you anyway, Dave.

a15_0700000.speaker: Scott
a15_0700000.text: Okay. Felt pretty good. We'll get organized and give you a call here in a few minutes.

a15_0700000.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0700000.text: Our spacecraft communicator at the moment is astronaut Bob Parker and he'll be replaced shortly by the oncoming CapCom, astronaut Joe Allen. There will be a change of shift press briefing. We expect that it will begin at about 7:15 or shortly thereafter in the News Center briefing room.

a15_0702605.speaker: Scott
a15_0702605.text: Good morning. I have a consumables report for you, and sleep report.

a15_0702605.speaker: Scott
a15_0702605.text: Okay. On the Commander: PRD - 7½ hours sleep; CMP: 25012, same sleep; LMP: 08013, same amount of sleep. On the consumables: At 70:15 [GET]: RCS; [quad A to D] 90 [per cent remaining], 87, 84, and 88. On the H 2 [tanks 1 to 3]; 90 [per cent remaining], 89, and 60. O 2 [tanks 1 to 3]; 88 [per cent remaining], 89, and 65. Over.

a15_0702605.speaker: Parker
a15_0702605.text: Roger. And, before I read that back, we did not catch the Commander's PRD reading. [Pause.]

a15_0702605.speaker: Parker
a15_0702605.text: Roger. Copy. Understand we have Commander's PRD 23046, 7½ hours sleep for all three crewmen; 25012 for the CMP; and 08013 for the LMP. And we have consumables update, based on our figures from the ground. For 70:00, we have [RCS] 84 per cent total, and we have [quad A to D] 85, 84, 84 and 85. And for H 2 [tank 1 to 3] we have 91, 90 and 60. For O 2 [tank 1 to 3] we have 89, 90 and 73. Over. [Pause.]

a15_0702605.speaker: Irwin
a15_0702605.text: Roger. I - I'm ready for any Flight Plan updates you might have.

a15_0702605.speaker: Parker
a15_0702605.text: Okay. First we have Flight Plan update for the day. We'll start out at - Stand by.

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: 15, Houston. You back with us again? [Pause.]

a15_0703121.speaker: Irwin
a15_0703121.text: Roger. We've been here all along, Bob.

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: Rog. We had the usual signal break when we went around in PTC there. Let me ask you one question. The EECOMs are interested in getting a verification on the O 2 tank 3 read-out, since there's a difference of 8 percent there. And, then after we get that, we'll proceed with this update. It's a fairly long one, so I guess you may as well...

a15_0703121.speaker: Irwin
a15_0703121.text: Okay. Stand by.

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: ...drag out your Flight Plan. [Long pause.]

a15_0703121.speaker: Irwin
a15_0703121.text: Okay. We're reading - 74 onboard.

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: Roger. Understand 74. Okay, Jim. And we'll start this Flight Plan update at 71 hours, so you can tell me when you get there. [Pause.]

a15_0703121.speaker: Irwin
a15_0703121.text: Okay. I'm there.

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: All right. At 71 hours, you want to add the following information. "High Gain Antenna [HGA] on MSFN cue," and note that we won't stop PTC. We'll have to give you the numbers [for the HGA angles], depending on where you are - in PTC, as we come around at this point. Second line is "S-band Aux TV, to Science, Pan Camera Mode, to Standby." That's a "Verify." "Pan Camera, Power, On. Pan Camera Self Test, to Heaters. Mapping Camera, On, to Standby. Then after five minutes, Pan Camera Power, Off, and S-band Aux, TV, Off." Copy? [Long pause.]

a15_0703121.speaker: Irwin
a15_0703121.text: Okay. Here's the readback, Bob. At 71 hours, "High Gain Antenna on MSFN cue, S-band Aux TV, to Science, Pan Camera Mode, to Standby." That's a "Verify." "Pan Camera Power, On; Pan Camera Self Test, to Heaters; Mapping Camera, On, to Standby; after five minutes, Pan Camera, Off, and S-band Aux, TV, Off."

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: Roger. That's good. Okay. Next item at 71:15. This will be a line added in after the "CM/LM Pressure Equalization Decal." And the line says, "Press Equal valve, Close." Over. [Pause.]

a15_0703121.speaker: Irwin
a15_0703121.text: Roger. At 71:15, "Pressure Equalization valve, Close."

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: Roger. And next one's on 73 hours and 15 minutes. [Pause.]

a15_0703121.speaker: Irwin
a15_0703121.text: Okay. Go.

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: Okay. And at 73:15, we will delete the line referring to waste water dump. "Waste Water Dump" will be deleted. [Pause.]

a15_0703121.speaker: Irwin
a15_0703121.text: Okay. I copy. Delete the "Waste Water Dump."

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: Okay. Next one will be at 81:42. 8 1 4 2. [Long pause.]

a15_0703121.speaker: Irwin
a15_0703121.text: Go.

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: Okay. And, in the configuration for the camera there, we're changing that from "CM4" to "CM3" on the second line. [Pause.]

a15_0703121.speaker: Irwin
a15_0703121.text: Okay. "CM3" is [garble] to "CM4."

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: Roger. Next one's on 84:24, 8 4 2 4. [Long pause.]

a15_0703121.speaker: Irwin
a15_0703121.text: Okay; go.

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: Roger. [This] also [concerns the] configuration of the camera, and we'll change that one also to "CM3" instead of "CM4." [Pause.]

a15_0703121.speaker: Irwin
a15_0703121.text: I copy.

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: Roger. And then over on the other side of the page at 84:40, again terminator photos. The first one, the first line there 84:40 will now read "EL, On" and the time will be "T start minus 1:40," one, four, zero. [Pause.]

a15_0703121.speaker: Irwin
a15_0703121.text: Okay. I copy.

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: And then at 84:42, "EL, Off" will now be at "EL, Off, parenthesis, T-start." [Pause.]

a15_0703121.speaker: Irwin
a15_0703121.text: I copy.

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: Okay. And we have two general notes. One refers to SIM [bay] door Jett[ison], and it's a reminder that we verify that the Lexan shield is mounted in - window 5, with the cardboard shade off, for a photograph of SIM door Jett. At - this is about 74 hours. [Pause.]

a15_0703121.speaker: Irwin
a15_0703121.text: Okay. Understand.

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: Okay, and second one is with respect to the Optics Cal[ibration]. And I guess that we should explain here that - people are wringing their hands down here about the fact the we looked at a little bit of a bias drift when you guys zeroed the optics the first day, and we sent up some procedures yesterday saying to be careful when you are doing it for P23. And then everybody else got - decided that we ought to be careful when we did it for other things besides P23. And so, we have the following procedures, which are, basically, to avoid high trunnion rates for all optics zeroing, so that we don't

a15_0703121.speaker: Irwin
a15_0703121.text: Okay, Bob. If Optics power Off, then Optics Zero switch, Zero? [Pause.]

a15_0703121.speaker: Parker
a15_0703121.text: Roger. It really is, "if Optics power Off, place the Zero switch to Off before turning the Optics power On."

a15_0704216.speaker: Irwin
a15_0704216.text: Bob, would you read that procedure again? Make sure I have it correct. I have Optics power, Off, then Optics Zero switch, Zero.

a15_0704216.speaker: Parker
a15_0704216.text: Okay, Jim. The thing is, if your Optics power is Off, we - as it will be like this morning, and the Zero switch is already on, as it probably is this morning, we want you to place the Zero switch to Off before you turn the Optics power on, because, otherwise, it will then automatically zero without you having any control over it. Do you understand? [Pause.]

a15_0704216.speaker: Irwin
a15_0704216.text: Read the - read the rest of it after the Op...

a15_0704216.speaker: Parker
a15_0704216.text: Okay. And then after, - Okay; I'll - I'll read it through from the beginning again. "If Optics power off, place Zero switch, Off, before turning Optics power On. Then, drive Optics manually to Trunnion less than 10 degrees before placing Zero switch, On." Over. [Long pause.]

a15_0704216.speaker: Irwin
a15_0704216.text: Okay. That was after the Optics power on. Drive optics until Trunnion is less than 10 degrees before Zero switch, On.

a15_0704216.speaker: Parker
a15_0704216.text: Roger. And the corollary to that is if the Optics power is already on, then we drive the Optics power manually to a Trunnion of less than 10 degrees before placing the Zero switch, On. That's the second part.

a15_0704216.speaker: Parker
a15_0704216.text: Okay. And then I have an update to your Contingency Checklist, page 4-3 which pertains to LOI burn rules if you can get that out.

a15_0704659.speaker: Irwin
a15_0704659.text: Okay, Bob. I have the Contingency Checklist.

a15_0704659.speaker: Parker
a15_0704659.text: Okay. And these changes are basically in the table there. - We'll start out under the heading of "Burn time." And that first one will be change from "00 to 1:36," now, instead of "1:35." So, it'll be 1:36 in the first burn time. The second line will be "1:36 to 1:57." And the third line will be "1:57 to 2:13." And the fourth line will be "2:13 to 3:11." Over. [Pause.]

a15_0704659.speaker: Parker
a15_0704659.text: Okay, the next one in the second column, "Delta-V M ," the lines will be 0 to, or "0-640, 640-784, 784-900, 900-1313." Over. [Pause.]

a15_0704659.speaker: Parker
a15_0704659.text: Okay, and, in the second block, the lower block, under the updates for the times and angles, we have the following readings under the "Update" column. The GET [Ground Elapsed Time] of LOI ignition is "78:31:34.2," the second time is "79:01:34.2," and the angles are "144, 358, and 68." Over. [Pause.]

a15_0704659.speaker: Irwin
a15_0704659.text: Okay, copied on the update time, "78:31:34.2, 79:01:34.2; 144, 358, and 68."

a15_0704659.speaker: Parker
a15_0704659.text: Roger. And, be advised, this also changes your little graph over on the side there. Primarily what it does, is to enlarge the mode 130 region by about 10 feet per second on either side and it changes the "LOI plus 30 abort Delta-V" line by essentially extending it and raising the left-hand corner just a wee bit. We could read up the lines too, if you want, but I'm not sure you really need those. Over. [Pause.]

a15_0704659.speaker: Parker
a15_0704659.text: We're coming up on another Omni switch, and we'll be back with you in a minute, Jim.

a15_0704659.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0704659.text: And this is Apollo Control; as we come up through a rotation of Passive Thermal Control and lose lock with one of the Omni[-directional] antennas. We'll take the circuit down in the next few moments to prepare for change of shift press conference in the Newsroom briefing room, Building 1. The distance from the Moon now 18,674 feet per sec [correcting himself] - nautical miles [34,584 km]; approaching the Moon at 3,797 feet per second [1,157 m/s]. Any air-to-ground conversation between Mission Control and the crew of Apollo 15 taking place during the change of shift press conference with Black

a15_0705317.speaker: Parker
a15_0705317.text: Okay, 15; we're back with you. [Long pause.]

a15_0705317.speaker: Parker
a15_0705317.text: Okay. Understand you really - didn't feel you needed the complete update to that graph, Jim. [Long pause.]

a15_0705317.speaker: Parker
a15_0705317.text: Jim, this is Houston. Is that a verify on the fact that you don't want the update on the graph? Over.

a15_0705317.speaker: Irwin
a15_0705317.text: I think we can do it ourselves, Bob.

a15_0705317.speaker: Parker
a15_0705317.text: Oh, Rog. Okay, and that's all the update we have for you at the moment. You might be interested in knowing that that water dump you guys scheduled last night before you went to bed, was at a very opportune time. Your PTC shifted plus or minus 2½ degrees all night.

a15_0705317.speaker: Parker
a15_0705317.text: We'll be up with the news in a while.

a15_0710130.speaker: Parker
a15_0710130.text: 15, Houston. We have a Pitch of minus 30 and a Yaw of 85 for the High Gain Antenna, and we'll give you a mark when to go.

a15_0710130.speaker: Parker
a15_0710130.text: And, 15, we're getting you on High Gain and receiving...

a15_0710130.speaker: Irwin
a15_0710130.text: Okay; we understand you're getting the data.

a15_0710130.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0710130.text: This is Apollo Control again. Hopefully the line is up properly. Every 2 hours the spacecraft analysis room [SPAN room] in the back of the Mission Control Center here prepares a report on the status of spacecraft systems. The report issued at 70 hours Ground Elapsed Time, a little over an hour ago, is very short; about three quarters of a page; the entries under thermal, displays and controls, instrumentation, power distribution and sequencing, communication, crew systems, guidance and control, propulsion and power; all have entries such as: 'No change in status,' 'Our systems performance has

a15_0711133.speaker: Irwin
a15_0711133.text: Roger. We just want to confirm the position of the switches on the Mapping Camera and Pan Camera. We have the "Mapping Camera On" is Standby, and the "Pan Camera, Power," Off. Is that correct?

a15_0711133.speaker: Parker
a15_0711133.text: Rog. If you finished [the procedure], that's the correct position.

a15_0711345.speaker: Parker
a15_0711345.text: 15. We'll take Omni Delta at this time please.

a15_0711345.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0711345.text: Now live on air-ground with Apollo 15

a15_0711851.speaker: Parker
a15_0711851.text: And, 15, we'd like Wide and Manual on High Gain [Antenna], please.

a15_0712400.speaker: Allen
a15_0712400.text: Apollo 15, this is Houston. Select Omni Bravo, please.

a15_0713425.speaker: Allen
a15_0713425.text: Stand by, Jim. I'll wait until the comm's a little better.

a15_0713901.speaker: Allen
a15_0713901.text: Good morning, Jim. This is your friendly News Reporter on duty now. And I wondered if you'd be interested in something from the local newspapers?

a15_0713901.speaker: Allen
a15_0713901.text: Roger. This is from the MOCR Gold Bugle and Taglich Zeitung News. The Administration effort to rescue Lockheed Aircraft cleared a major hurdle in the Senate yesterday when an amendment to deny favored status was rejected 60 to 35. Houston unemployment rose to 4.1 per cent in June, an increase of a full percentage point from May, which is the highest in 6 years. And this morning's Post reports that the checkout of Falcon went on with a few words from Worden and virtually nothing from the other astronauts. However, I think that's incorrect and I enjoyed talking to you very much yesterday. In spo

a15_0713901.speaker: Allen
a15_0713901.text: Al, this is Houston. And we're standing by for your null bias EMS check if you've gotten to that yet.

a15_0713901.speaker: Worden
a15_0713901.text: Rog. The Delta-V test was good, and the null bias was 1.0.

a15_0714916.speaker: Allen
a15_0714916.text: Roger, Jim. Just wanted to tell you to expect all your updates on time except the PAD; and we're going to delay the PAD to 72 [hours] plus 50 [minutes] because of very good tracking data we'll be getting in those last few extra minutes there.

a15_0714916.speaker: Irwin
a15_0714916.text: Okay; understand. Expect the PAD about 72:50.

a15_0720421.speaker: Allen
a15_0720421.text: Go ahead, 15. This is Houston. We hear you now.

a15_0720421.speaker: Worden
a15_0720421.text: Morning, José. Say, listen; on this - on the door jettison photography, we've got about 50 per cent left on mag[azine] A, and we thought we would go ahead and use that. [Pause.]

a15_0720421.speaker: Allen
a15_0720421.text: Good morning, Alfredo. We copied you, but I'm not sure that I understand your question.

a15_0720421.speaker: Worden
a15_0720421.text: Okay, Joe. No, it's not a question. Just wanted to let you know, on the 16 millimeter photography for the SIM door jett, the Flight Plan called out mag - stand by one. Yeah; it called out mag Echo, and we're going to use mag Alpha instead. We['ve] got about 50 per cent left on it. Just letting you know.

a15_0720421.speaker: Allen
a15_0720421.text: Okay, Al. Thank you. And, by the way, is that the maneuver where the SIM bay door jettisons the spacecraft?

a15_0720421.speaker: Worden
a15_0720421.text: It's been variously known as that kind of a maneuver, yeah.

a15_0720421.speaker: Allen
a15_0720421.text: Roger. I'm looking forward to that.

a15_0720421.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0720421.text: This is Apollo Control. Everything this morning [is] going along on schedule. Next major event in the mission will be the midcourse correction number 4 maneuver, at the nominal Flight Plan time of 73 hours, 31 minutes, 14 seconds. Looking at a desired velocity change of 5.3 feet per second [1.6 m/s]. The burn will be with the Service Propulsion System on bank B only. All other major burns of the SPS and, in and out of lunar orbit will be made with both banks, bank A having to be switched on manually. Following the midcourse correction, the SIM door jettison; that is the Scientific Instrument M

a15_0722213.speaker: Allen
a15_0722213.text: Roger, 15. I have a maneuver PAD, PC plus 2, when you're ready to copy.

a15_0722213.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0722213.text: This is Apollo Control. The PC plus 2, the PAD referred to by spacecraft communicator, Joe Allen, is the Pericynthion plus 2-hours Abort PAD, which would be a maneuver...

a15_0722213.speaker: Worden
a15_0722213.text: Okay, Joe. I'm ready; go ahead.

a15_0722213.speaker: Allen
a15_0722213.text: Roger. PC plus 2, SPS/G&N. 66313; plus 1.23, minus 0.12; 080:29:13.47; plus 3189.4, minus 2437.0, minus 1356.5; 175, 079, 332; all other is NA; ullage, none; other, burn equals SPS docked. Over.

a15_0722213.speaker: Worden
a15_0722213.text: Roger, Joe; copy. Plane change plus 2, SPS/G&N; 66313, plus 1.23, minus 0.12; 080:29:13.47; plus 3189.4, minus 2437.0, minus 1356.5; 175, 079, 332; no ullage; and that burn equals SPS docked.

a15_0722213.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0722213.text: This is Apollo Control. To recapitulate, the Pericynthion plus 2-hour Abort PAD, read up to the crew; ignition time for such an abort, should it become necessary, would be at 80 hours, 29 minutes, 13.47 seconds Ground Elapsed Time, would be a docked burn with the Lunar Module still attached, using the Service Propulsion System. Total velocity change, posigrade 3,189.4 feet per second. Should be getting the maneuver PAD up to the crew before too long for midcourse number 4 at 73 hours, 31 minutes ignition time. Standing by live on air/ground; this is Apollo Control at 72:27.

a15_0723844.speaker: Allen
a15_0723844.text: Apollo 15, this is Houston. We need P00 and Accept to give you a state vector and a target load, and we'll uplink when we get the next Omni. [Pause.]

a15_0724238.speaker: Allen
a15_0724238.text: Apollo 15. This is Houston with the maneuver PAD [for] midcourse 4, when you're ready.

a15_0724238.speaker: Irwin
a15_0724238.text: Okay, Joe. I'm ready to copy the midcourse 4 PAD.

a15_0724238.speaker: Allen
a15_0724238.text: Roger, Jim. Midcourse 4, SPS/G&N; 66531, plus 1.23, minus 0.12; 073:31:14.02; plus 0001.9, minus 0003.6, plus 0003.5; 038, 240, 331 - [Apollo] 15, hold off the P52; we're commanding, and go to P00 and Accept, please.

a15_0724238.speaker: Irwin
a15_0724238.text: Okay. We - we're back in P00 and Accept. I forgot, there's no uplink activity light in the LEB.

a15_0724238.speaker: Allen
a15_0724238.text: Roger, 15. I'll continue with the PAD. H A is NA, NA; 0005.4, 0:01, 0003.2; 23, 106.1, 17.6. The rest is NA. GDC Align, Vega, Deneb; roll align, 209, 009, 349; ullage, none. Other: LM weight, 36256; SIM door jett attitude is nominal. Single bank Bravo burn. High Gain: Pitch, 21 [degrees]; Yaw, 243. Over.

a15_0724238.speaker: Irwin
a15_0724238.text: Okay, Joe. Readback for midcourse 4, SPS/G&N; 66531; plus 1.23, minus 0.12; 073:31:14.02; plus 0001.9, minus 0003.6, plus 0003.5; 038, 240, 331; 0005.4, 0:01, 0003.2; 23, 106.1, 17.6. Vega and Deneb; 209; 009; 349. No ullage. LM weight, 36256; SIM door Jett, attitude nominal. Single bank burn on Bravo. High Gain: Pitch, 21; Yaw, 243.

a15_0724238.speaker: Allen
a15_0724238.text: Roger, Jim. Sounds good, and it's your computer.

a15_0724238.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0724238.text: This is Apollo Control. To recap the numbers just read up to the crew of Apollo 15 by their spacecraft communicator, this is a so-called maneuver PAD for the midcourse correction burn number 4 with a time of ignition of 73 hours, 31 minutes, 14 seconds. Total velocity change of 5.4 feet per second [1.65 m/s]. Burn time: 1 second and it'll be with the Service Propulsion System on Bank B. Rejoining somewhat scratchy air/ground as we drift through from one Omni antenna to the other. This is Apollo Control.

a15_0725033.speaker: Scott
a15_0725033.text: Okay, Houston. Gimbal angles are up [on the DSKY display]. We'll torque them on the minute.

a15_0725033.speaker: Scott
a15_0725033.text: Houston, 15. Did you get the gyro torquing angles?

a15_0725033.speaker: Allen
a15_0725033.text: Roger, Dave. We got them. Thank you.

a15_0731229.speaker: Allen
a15_0731229.text: Apollo 15, Houston. Requesting the High Gain [Antenna], when convenient. [Pause.]

a15_0731627.speaker: Allen
a15_0731627.text: Apollo 15, Houston. Just a reminder to load the DAP and then go on back. [Pause.]

a15_0733106.speaker: Scott
a15_0733106.text: Okay, Houston. [Apollo] 15 with the burn status report.

a15_0733106.speaker: Allen
a15_0733106.text: Go ahead, Dave. This is Houston.

a15_0733106.speaker: Scott
a15_0733106.text: Okay. I guess you could see it was a nice smooth burn. On time. Burn time was a second. Delta-V GX at the end of the burn was .2 [feet per second]; there was no trim; residuals were plus .2, minus .1, plus .1; Delta-V C was a minus 2.3.

a15_0733106.speaker: Allen
a15_0733106.text: Roger, Dave. We copy. And we think you're bragging, but you have a reason to. Beautiful burn.

a15_0733106.speaker: Scott
a15_0733106.text: It's all this nice machinery up here, Joe.

a15_0733106.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0733106.text: This is Apollo Control. Midcourse maneuver number 4 was on time; burn time of eighty one hundredths of one second [actual is 91 hundredths of a second]. Crew reported no residuals or no trim: that is no tweaking maneuvers to take out any errors or dispersions in the burn. Apollo 15 is now 12,421 nautical miles [23,004 km] out from the Moon, approaching at a velocity of 3,974 feet per second [1,211 m/s]. Crew coming up on a suit circuit integrity check in preparation for jettisoning the SIM bay door, that is the panel covering the Scientific Instrument Module in the - back in the Service Module

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: Okay; Houston, 15.

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Roger. Go ahead.

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: Okay. Suit pressure integrity check is okay. The flow was about .3 or .4 [pounds per minute]. And we're proceeding into the setup for the SIM bay door jettison, and we'll give you a call when we get everything ready before we blow it.

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Roger, Dave. Sounds good.

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: Houston, this is 15. We're ready to turn Pan Camera Power, On, if you are. [Pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Roger, Jim. Go ahead.

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: Okay. It's coming on now.

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: 15, Houston. [Pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Jim, we're not sure that the cameras are running properly. We want you to check the two SEB circuit breakers on panel 5, In, and confirm for us that you got the right talkback when you turned them On. [Pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: The two circuit breakers on panel 5 are in. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: Joe, there's no talkback called out here on the [line in the checklist which says] "Pan Camera Power, On." [Long pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Roger. We copy. [Pause.] And, Jim, apparently, when you turn the power on, you should get about 2 seconds of barber pole, and then back to gray. It may very well have happened and you just didn't notice it.

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: Okay. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: Houston, this is 15. Do you want us to turn the Pan Camera Power on again and check that talkback a little more carefully? [Long pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Jim, that sounds like a good...

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: Houston, 15.

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: ...idea to us. Would you turn the Pan Camera Power off, wait 30 seconds, and then go back on, watching the barber - the - for the barber pole indication, please.

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: Okay, that's in work.

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: Houston, this is 15.

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Roger. Go ahead.

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: Roger. We have the SM/AC Power, Off, down on 180 [sic], per the P40 checklist. Should we put that power on?

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Jim, that's affirm. That power should be on, and that's probably our problem. Thank you.

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0735237.text: This is Apollo Control. The SIM [bay] door jettison has been delayed momentarily, until the switches are in the proper position; getting power to the SIM cameras down in the SIM Bay. It's not a time critical event.

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: Okay, Houston. The SM/AC Power is On, and the Pan Cameras are [means singular] coming back to power at this time.

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Roger.

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: And we got a barber pole for 2 seconds. [Pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Roger. As advertised. Thank you, Dave. [Pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: Okay. I guess that's a spot in the clean-up of the P40 that didn't get carried over to the Flight Plan.

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: We concur. [Long pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: 15, verify Map Camera, Standby, please. [Pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: Stand by. Okay; Mapping Camera going Standby.

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: The - the Mapping Camera is in Standby now, but required a - a change. [Long pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: Okay; Houston, 15. I - do you want the Mapping Camera in Standby for the door jett.

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: That's affirmative, 15. Map Camera, Standby. [Pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: Houston, would you like the SM sector AC Power, Off, for the SIM door jettison?

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: That's right, Jim. Per the checklist, the first one in step four.

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: Okay. We just wanted to confirm it.

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Roger. Sounds like a good idea. I think we have a bug or two in this procedure. [Long pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Apollo 15, Houston. [Pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: Go ahead, Houston,

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Roger, Dave. We're ready for Pan Camera Power to Boost. On your step 2 there, you are Go for SIM door jettison. And we want you to watch the Fuel Cell Reactant valves after the jettison, per the checklist - just a reminder of that. Over.

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: Okay; understand. And we are in Boost, and we'll give you a mark when we blow the door.

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Roger. And we will be standing by for a description.

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: Okay, Houston; 15. SIM [bay] door jett. - 3, 2, 1...

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: Mark.

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: [I] felt a little shudder, but not too much.

a15_0735237.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0735237.text: This is Apollo Control. We mark the time of actual SIM [bay] door jettison at 74 hours, 6 minutes, 47 seconds. Rejoining live air to ground.

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: Okay, Houston. We have negative visual on the SIM door as of yet. And the fuel cells looked okay. The RCS Bravo primary talkback went to barber pole and is reset, and otherwise no reaction in here.

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Roger, Dave. We copy. And we assume you didn't notice any debris of any kind either.

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: Nothing in particular, Joe, and Jim's got a visual now. [Long pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: Okay, Houston. Jim's got it out of his window, and he's taking pictures, and he says it's slowly tumbling.

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: And, 15, just out of interest, we saw a good healthy jolt in our Doppler data down here during jett time.

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: Gee, that's very interesting because I would say that the jolt in here was very minor. [Long pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Scott
a15_0735237.text: Houston, 15. I guess the consensus would say that the - the shock was about one-tenth of the other pyros we've seen up to this point.

a15_0735237.speaker: Allen
a15_0735237.text: Roger, Dave. We copy. Can you still see the world's largest lens cap [the SIM bay door] out the window? [Pause.]

a15_0735237.speaker: Irwin
a15_0735237.text: We'll check.

a15_0735237.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0735237.text: This is Apollo Control. Some distance and velocity figures. Altitude now 10,915 nautical miles [20,215 km] out from the Moon. Approaching at a velocity of 4,042 feet per second [1,232 m/s]. Successful jettison of the SIM bay door at 74:06:47; a few moments late because of getting into the right power set-up for the equipment in the SIM bay, primarily the Mapping and Panoramic Cameras. We rejoin the air/ground as it proceeds toward Lunar Orbit Insertion later today. At 74 hours, 16 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

a15_0743447.speaker: Allen
a15_0743447.text: Roger. We've looked ahead in - several hours in our Flight Plan, and we've - see no further inconsistencies between the checklist and the Flight Plan like the small problem we just had with the power. So, just wanted to advise you of - of this, and just follow the Flight Plan as usual. Over.

a15_0743447.speaker: Worden
a15_0743447.text: Okay, Joe; we'll follow the cookbook. Thank you.

a15_0743447.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0743447.text: This is Apollo Control. Apollo 15 just crossed the 10 thousand [nautical] mile mark in its approach to the Moon. Distance now 9,975 nautical miles [18,474 km] out. Velocity; 4,092 feet per second [1,247 m/s].

a15_0744947.speaker: Allen
a15_0744947.text: Roger. I've got a preliminary maneuver PAD for LOI [Lunar Orbit Insertion] when you're ready.

a15_0744947.speaker: Allen
a15_0744947.text: And, Apollo 15, if you'll give us P00 and Accept, please, we'll give you a preliminary state vector, target load, and a REFSMMAT.

a15_0744947.speaker: Irwin
a15_0744947.text: Okay; you've got P00 and Accept.

a15_0744947.speaker: Irwin
a15_0744947.text: And I'm ready to copy the preliminary PAD, Joe.

a15_0744947.speaker: Allen
a15_0744947.text: Roger, Jim. Just out of curiosity, has the SIM bay door long since disappeared from view?

a15_0744947.speaker: Irwin
a15_0744947.text: Yes, I looked for it a few minutes ago and couldn't see it any longer.

a15_0744947.speaker: Allen
a15_0744947.text: Okay, thank you. And I'll go ahead with the maneuver PAD. LOI, SPS/G&N; 66244; plus 1.21, minus 0.12; 078:31:34.48; minus 2894.5, minus 0766.4, minus 0112.3; Roll, pitch and yaw, all zips. 0169.5, plus 0058.3; 2996.4, 6:40, 2990.2; 25, 267.1, 228. The rest is NA. GDC Align, Vega - Deneb on zero degrees mark. Roll align, 264; 090; 349. No ullage. LM weight, 36258. Over. [Pause.]

a15_0744947.speaker: Irwin
a15_0744947.text: Roger, Joe. Readback for LOI: SPS/G&N; 66244; plus 1.21; minus 0.12; 078:31:34.48; minus 2894.5, minus 0766.4, minus 0112.3. All zips for roll, pitch and yaw. 0169.5, plus 0058.3; 2996.4, 6:40, 2990.2; 25, 267.1, 228. Vega and Deneb on the zero mark. 264, 090, and 349. No ullage. LM weight, 36258.

a15_0744947.speaker: Allen
a15_0744947.text: That sounds good, Jim. Thank you.

a15_0744947.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0744947.text: This is Apollo Control. To translate what that stream of numbers means, it's a preliminary maneuver PAD for the Lunar Orbit Insertion maneuver later on today. With a time of ignition at - as it stands now of 78 hours, 31 minutes, 34 seconds. Velocity change, retrograde that is, of 2,996 feet per second [913 m/s]. Burn time; 6 minutes, 40 seconds, which would produce a lunar orbit for the pericynthion of 58.3 nautical miles [108 km], apocynthion of 169.5 nautical miles [313.9 km]. Apollo 15 now 9,269 nautical miles [17,166 km] out from Earth [means Moon]. Velocity; 4,137 feet per second [1,261

a15_0751519.speaker: Scott
a15_0751519.text: Houston, 15. The first P52 is complete, and I trust you got the torquing angles. [Pause.]

a15_0751519.speaker: Scott
a15_0751519.text: Okay, and processing the second one [the second P52 realignment].

a15_0751519.speaker: Allen
a15_0751519.text: Dave, did you copy? We got the torquing angles. Thank you.

a15_0751519.speaker: Scott
a15_0751519.text: Okay, and the second P52 is in work.

a15_0751915.speaker: Scott
a15_0751915.text: Okay, Houston; 15. The second P52 torqued out at 75:19 [GET].

a15_0751915.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0751915.text: This is Apollo Control at 76 hours, 08 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 15 crew rather quiet during the past hour or more as they coast in toward the Moon. They're now 6,331 nautical miles [11,725 km] out from the Moon. Velocity continuing to build up; now showing 4,401 feet per second [1,341 m/s]. Here's a call now from the crew.

a15_0760813.speaker: Worden
a15_0760813.text: Rog, Joe. Delta-V test, Null Bias Check. The null bias is 1 foot per second per 100 seconds.

a15_0760813.speaker: Allen
a15_0760813.text: Okay, Al. We copy. Thank you.

a15_0760813.speaker: Allen
a15_0760813.text: And, Al, you'll be interested to know that the SIM bay data we're getting so far looks very good.

a15_0760813.speaker: Worden
a15_0760813.text: Okay, Joe. And you'll be interested to know that there's a very thin, crescent Moon in front of us.

a15_0760813.speaker: Allen
a15_0760813.text: Roger. We've been suspecting that all along. [Pause.]

a15_0760813.speaker: Worden
a15_0760813.text: And it may be thin, but it's big.

a15_0760813.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0760813.text: This is Apollo Control at 76 hours, 11 minutes. We're in the process of a shift change in the Control Center now. Flight Director Milt Windler and his team relieving Gerry Griffin and his team of flight controllers. We estimate the change of shift news conference for 1 pm Central Daylight Time. 1 pm Central Daylight Time for the the change of shift news conference.

a15_0760813.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0760813.text: This is Apollo Control at 76 hours, 24 minutes. Change of shift news conference is about to begin. We'll take the air/ground off the release line and tape for replay after the news conference.

a15_0760813.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0760813.text: This is Apollo Control at 76 hours, 39 minutes. Apollo 15 is 5,003 nautical miles [9,266 km] from the Moon, velocity; 4,595 feet per second [1,401 m/s]. There were no air/ground conversations during the news conference. We're back up live now. We'll continue to monitor live.

a15_0763932.speaker: Irwin
a15_0763932.text: Houston, this is 15. The Pre-LOI Secondary Glycol loop check looked good.

a15_0763932.speaker: Henize
a15_0763932.text: And, 15, I have a TEI-4 PAD for you any time that you have time to copy it.

a15_0763932.speaker: Irwin
a15_0763932.text: Okay, Karl. I'm ready to copy the TEI-4 PAD.

a15_0763932.speaker: Henize
a15_0763932.text: Roger. TEI-4, SPS/G&N, 40015; plus 0.59, plus 1.21; 087:12:40.06; plus 3121.1, minus 2074.0, minus 0643.0; 182, 057, 329; the rest is NA. Ullage, 4 jets, 12 seconds, and this assumes burn undocked; and no DOI; and the roll, pitch, and yaw angles assume landing site REFSMMAT. And that's all.

a15_0763932.speaker: Goddard
a15_0763932.text: NASA Headquarters, Goddard voice of Net 1.

a15_0763932.speaker: Irwin
a15_0763932.text: ...6; plus 3121.1, minus 2074.0, minus 0643.0; 182, 057, 329; 4 jets, 12 seconds, assumes burn undocked; and no DOI; landing site REFSMMAT.

a15_0763932.speaker: Henize
a15_0763932.text: Roger, Jim. The part [of the readback] I got was correct, but we had a loss of comm for the first part. Would you read the - about the first 10 [items] back to me again.

a15_0763932.speaker: Irwin
a15_0763932.text: Houston, this is 15. Did you get all the readback?

a15_0763932.speaker: Henize
a15_0763932.text: 15, this is Houston. We're having a comm problem down here on the ground and I need to check still your Noun 48 and your Noun 33.

a15_0770218.speaker: Scott
a15_0770218.text: Roger, Karl. All the systems checks are complete and everything looks good.

a15_0770218.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0770218.text: This is Apollo Control at 77 hours, 08 minutes. Apollo 15 now 3,728 nautical miles [6,904 km] from the Moon. Velocity; 4,875 feet per second [1,486 m/s]. The Flight Dynamics Officer [FIDO] has just provided the Flight Director with some times. We expect Loss Of Signal [LOS] as Apollo 15 goes behind the Moon at 78 hours, 23 minutes, 31 seconds. If the Lunar Orbit Insertion burn is not performed, we should acquire the spacecraft signal at 78 hours, 46 minutes, 43 seconds. If we have a nominal LOI burn, we should acquire at 78 hours, 55 minutes, 09 seconds. The FIDO has also taken the final vecto

a15_0770218.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0770218.text: This is Apollo Control at 77 hours, 23 minutes. We're 1 hour away from LOS now. And Apollo 15 is 3,044 [nautical] miles [5,637 km] from the Moon. Velocity; 5,083 feet per second [1,549 m/s]. We're 1 hour, 7 minutes, 42 seconds away from the Lunar Orbit Insertion burn which will be performed behind the Moon.

a15_0772332.speaker: Scott
a15_0772332.text: Houston, Apollo 15.

a15_0772332.speaker: Henize
a15_0772332.text: 15, go ahead. [No answer.]

a15_0772332.speaker: Henize
a15_0772332.text: 15, this is Houston. Go ahead.

a15_0772332.speaker: Scott
a15_0772332.text: Houston, Apollo 15.

a15_0772332.speaker: Henize
a15_0772332.text: 15, this is Houston. Go ahead.

a15_0772332.speaker: Scott
a15_0772332.text: Okay. We've just made a little mission-rules review up here, and I have one question for you - relative to the circuit breaker on bank A procedure at 6 minutes. Our interpretation of the mission rules says that, if we have a bank B ball valve close prematurely, then we would leave that circuit breaker closed until shutdown, and close - or - until 10 seconds prior to shutdown, using that as our good bank rather than closing it in 6 minutes. And this is in reference to the cue card - at the bottom where it discusses one ball valve closing prematurely. [Pause.]

a15_0772332.speaker: Henize
a15_0772332.text: Stand by.

a15_0772332.speaker: Scott
a15_0772332.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a15_0772332.speaker: Scott
a15_0772332.text: Houston 15. I'll just repeat it once here, maybe in simpler terms. If bank B closes prematurely, then we'll leave the Pilot Valve [circuit breaker] on A closed until 10 seconds prior to cut-off, instead of at 6 minutes.

a15_0772332.speaker: Henize
a15_0772332.text: Roger, we copy. [Long pause.]

a15_0772332.speaker: Henize
a15_0772332.text: 15, Houston. We copy your question and we concur.

a15_0772332.speaker: Scott
a15_0772332.text: Okay, thank you. Everything else, I think, we have squared away.

a15_0772332.speaker: Henize
a15_0772332.text: Roger. Milt [Windler, Flight Director] says we owed you a review before every burn. Are you interested in a quick run through of what happens at LOI?

a15_0772332.speaker: Scott
a15_0772332.text: Sure, why not. Let's do it.

a15_0772332.speaker: Henize
a15_0772332.text: Okay. As I have it here, starting at T minus 2 - T minus 2 minutes, we close the Main B Pilot Valve circuit breaker. At T minus 5 seconds, we Pro[ceed, i.e. press the Proceed button on the DSKY]. Then the Delta-V Thrust A & B switches both go to Normal. At T plus 5 seconds, we Close the Main A Pilot Valve circuit breaker; and, at T plus 6 minutes, assuming nominal burns, we Open the Main A Pilot Valve circuit breaker; and, after that we avoid PUGS manipulation. And a reminder here is - don't forget to turn on the DSE because we're vitally interested in that single-engine [means single-bank] bu

a15_0772332.speaker: Scott
a15_0772332.text: Okay, Houston; we're right with you. We've just gone through that and - we understand it. Thank you.

a15_0772332.speaker: Henize
a15_0772332.text: Very good.

a15_0772332.speaker: Henize
a15_0772332.text: 15, this is Houston. If you'll give us Accept, we'll send up a new state vector.

a15_0772332.speaker: Scott
a15_0772332.text: Rog; you got it. P00 and Accept. [Pause.]

a15_0772332.speaker: Henize
a15_0772332.text: Okay; and I have an LOI PAD for you whenever you're ready to copy.

a15_0772332.speaker: Irwin
a15_0772332.text: Okay Karl, I'm ready to copy.

a15_0772332.speaker: Henize
a15_0772332.text: Okay. LOI, SPS/G&N; 66244; plus 1.21, minus 0.12; 078:31:45.91; minus 2897.5, minus 0776.4, minus 0044.1; all zips for roll, all zips for pitch, all zips for yaw; 0169.6, plus 0058.4, 3000.1, 6:41, 2993.9; 25, 267.1, 22.8; the rest is NA. Set stars are Vega and Deneb; 264, 090, 349. No ullage; LM weight 36258. Single-bank burn time is 6 plus 52; and just a reminder that, if bank B doesn't burn, we are expecting you to go into lunar orbit on bank A. [Long pause.]

a15_0772332.speaker: Irwin
a15_0772332.text: Okay, Karl. LOI PAD readback: SPS/G&N; 66244; plus 1.21, minus 0.12, 078:31:45.91; minus 2897.5, minus 0776.4, minus 0044.1; all zeros for roll, pitch, and yaw; 0169.6, plus 0058.4, 3000,1. 6:41, 2993.9; 25, 267.1, 22.8. Vega, Deneb; 264, 090, 349. No ullage. LM weight, 36258. Single-bank time, 6 plus 52.

a15_0772332.speaker: Henize
a15_0772332.text: That's all correct. [Pause.] And it's your computer now, 15.

a15_0772332.speaker: Irwin
a15_0772332.text: Rog. And we also understood that, if bank A doesn't light, we'll take it on in with Bank - I mean, if Bank B doesn't light, we'll take it on in with bank A, We don't need to discuss that.

a15_0772332.speaker: Henize
a15_0772332.text: Roger.

a15_0772332.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0772332.text: This is Apollo Control at 77 hours, 36 minutes. We've just passed up the final LOI burn PAD to the crew. Ignition time: 78 hours, 31 minutes, 45.91 seconds. Delta - Delta-V, or change in velocity of 3,000.1 feet per second [914.4 m/s]; burn time of 6 minutes, 41 seconds. The expected resulting orbital parameters: 169.6 by 58.4 nautical miles [314.1 by 108.2 km]. And the Flight Director has updated by a few seconds the acquisition times after LOI. The Loss of Signal time remains the same: 78 hours, 23 minutes, 31 seconds. The 'no burn' acquisition time is 78 hours, 46 minutes, 44 seconds. And t

a15_0773638.speaker: Henize
a15_0773638.text: 15, this is Houston. I have a map update, when you have time to copy. [Pause.]

a15_0774914.speaker: Irwin
a15_0774914.text: Houston, 15. I'm ready to copy the map update.

a15_0774914.speaker: Henize
a15_0774914.text: Roger, 15. I have four times for you, beginning with LOS. 78:23:31; 78:33:27; 78:55:03; 78:46:44. That's all. [Pause. ]

a15_0774914.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0774914.text: This is Apollo Control at 77 hours, 57 minutes. Telemetry shows that Apollo 15 has maneuvered to the - the maneuver attitude - [correcting himself] the burn attitude. Spacecraft is now 1,431 nautical miles [2,650 km] from the Moon and velocity has increased to 5,966 feet per second [1,818 m/s].

a15_0774914.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0774914.text: This is Apollo Control at 77 hours, 59 minutes. The Guidance, Navigation and Control Officer [GNC] reports now that Apollo 15 has completed the sextant star check.

a15_0780347.speaker: Henize
a15_0780347.text: 15, this is Houston. Everything is looking in good shape down here, and you have a Go for LOI. [Pause.]

a15_0780347.speaker: Scott
a15_0780347.text: Rog. Houston, 15. Understand. Go for LOI.

a15_0780347.speaker: Henize
a15_0780347.text: And a note here from EECOM that, due to destratification in your oxygen tanks, you may get a cryo pressure light; don't worry about it. That's during the burn.

a15_0780347.speaker: Scott
a15_0780347.text: Okay. Rog. Understand the cryo pressure.

a15_0780347.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0780347.text: This is Apollo Control at 78 hours, 7 minutes. Apollo 15, now, is less than 1,000 [nautical] miles from the Moon; distance, 985 nautical miles [1,824 km]. Velocity; 6,428 feet per second [1,959 m/s]. We're 15 minutes, 45 seconds away from Loss Of Signal as Apollo 15 will go behind the Moon. We're 23 minutes, 50 seconds away from ignition for the Lunar Orbit Insertion burn. At 78 hours, 08 minutes; this is Mission Control, Houston.

a15_0780347.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0780347.text: This is Apollo Control at 78 hours, 10 minutes. The viewing room behind the Mission Operations Control Room is beginning to fill up now, as we near the Loss Of Signal. All of the Flight Directors are beginning to assemble in the Control Room proper.

a15_0780347.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0780347.text: This is Apollo Control. We're 5 minutes away from Loss Of Signal now and Apollo 15 is 490 - 484 nautical miles [896 km] from the Moon. Velocity; 7,185 feet per second [2,190 m/s].

a15_0781829.speaker: Henize
a15_0781829.text: Gentlemen, everything looks perfect down here, and - all we can say is, "Have a good burn."

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: Okay, thank you. We'll see you on the other side.

a15_0781829.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0781829.text: And we've had Loss Of Signal. And at that time we showed Apollo 15 [at] 293 nautical miles [543 km] from the Moon. Velocity; 7,624 feet per second [2,324 m/s]. We'll take this line down now and come back up just prior to the no-burn acquisition time. That's 78 hours, 46 minutes, 44 seconds. We'll come up just prior to that time and stand by. At 78 hours, 24 minutes; this is Mission Control, Houston.

a15_0781829.speaker: Irwin
a15_0781829.text: You guys got all your oxygen?

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: Minus 5 and a Pro, and a Delta-V thrust of plus 5 ... Okay. Pilot Valve, open. Everything else looks good.

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: And we settle down for the Delta-V thrust.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: Okay. 99 Pro. Ought to be okay.

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: And the Delta-V Thrust is on.

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: ...A valves. P C is reading about 90.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: ... Okay. The EMS and the Delta-V and the DSKY look good. And we have tight limits. Very smooth.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: Okay, the DSKY and EMS look good. Still in the tight limits.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: A minute, and you're tracking Pitch 41.

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: Hmm! Right on, huh? Okay, the pressure's running 95; holding steady.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: Okay. Keep going on tight limits.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: The DSKY and the EMS agree. ... watch for the loose limits?

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: Yes. I should be able to ... loose limits.

a15_0781829.speaker: Irwin
a15_0781829.text: Five degrees, Dave. And the balance - unbalance is holding very well. About minus 180.

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: Right on the center of the roll dead band.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: Dead on it - right on the side of the roll.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: Not even on the side. It's only at 4 degrees.

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: We have a Pitch 34. It'll probably stretch out after we go to the single bank insertion.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: DSKY and EMS agree pretty well.

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: The DSKY and the EMS are about 12 feet per second difference - is all. That's pretty good.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: That view meter's not even registering.

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: Did you get your watch started on time, Jimmer?

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: Okay, because we need you to tell us at 6 minutes.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: How are the pressures looking over there, Jim?

a15_0781829.speaker: Irwin
a15_0781829.text: P C is reading 95 and holding steady.

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: Are we 12 feet per second - difference between the EMS and Delta-V?

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: Somebody would chew his ass if it didn't.

a15_0781829.speaker: Irwin
a15_0781829.text: P C is creeping up just a little bit.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: Okay. Should be approaching the tight limits, Jim.

a15_0781829.speaker: Irwin
a15_0781829.text: Okay, you're in tight limits now. About 2½ minutes to go.

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: P C 's about to cross over.

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: It crossed a little, but not much.

a15_0781829.speaker: Irwin
a15_0781829.text: Hey, listen. Your P C went up about 2 - about - 2 per cent, and it's up to about 98 now.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: Okay, the EMS and the DSKY are about 10 feet per second difference. We're at tight limits. About 2 minutes to go. G&N's tracking 638.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: Okay. EMS and the DSKY are within about 10 feet per second. Track at 638. Tight limits.

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: Okay. Give me a countdown at 6 minutes.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: You want Jim to count down at 6 minutes?

a15_0781829.speaker: Irwin
a15_0781829.text: You want me to give you a 10-second count?

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: A little dead band in there in the roll?

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: Okay, about 10 feet per second difference between the EMS and the DSKY, and we're looking good.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: P C 's varying between about 96 and 98. Looking good thoughl

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: Pilot Valve A is out. P C is down to 94.

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: Okay, we'll need another countdown to the...

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: Okay. Can you reach them there, Dave?

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: You've got 10 seconds overburn, don't forget.

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: Jim, Jim. Let's clean it up, Jim.

a15_0781829.speaker: Irwin
a15_0781829.text: Stand by for gimbal motors, Al.

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: I thought I just gave you one.

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: I'll try it again. All right, number one coming off.

a15_0781829.speaker: Irwin
a15_0781829.text: ...three, four. Okay. TVC Servo Power 1 and 2, Off.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: That is the best burn I've ever seen and I've seen 10, I mean 11. that isn't real! I've never seen one come out that good.

a15_0781829.speaker: Irwin
a15_0781829.text: Well, that's just superior cunning and skill, men.

a15_0781829.speaker: Scott
a15_0781829.text: Yes. It's got to be. Certainly (laughter).

a15_0781829.speaker: Worden
a15_0781829.text: Okay, Jim. Clean up the rest.

a15_0781829.speaker: Irwin
a15_0781829.text: Okay, you got all the data? Got the EMS data?

a15_0781829.speaker: Irwin
a15_0781829.text: ROT Control Power Direct, two, Off.

a15_0781829.speaker: Irwin
a15_0781829.text: CB SPS Pitch 1 and Yaw 1, open.

a15_0781829.speaker: Irwin
a15_0781829.text: SPS Pilot Valve Main B, open.

a15_0781829.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0781829.text: This is Apollo Control at 78 hours, 45 minutes. We're about a minute and a half away from the no-burn Acquisition Of Signal [AOS] time. If we get a signal at that time it will mean that Apollo 15 did not perform the Lunar Orbit Insertion burn. We're 9 minutes and 38 seconds away from acquisition time for a normal burn. Of course if we get a signal anytime between those two times, it will mean that Apollo 15 has had a partial Lunar Orbit Insertion burn. We'll stand by live through this period.

a15_0781829.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0781829.text: We're 15 seconds past the no-burn signal time now and still don't have a signal.

a15_0781829.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0781829.text: We're a minute and a half past the no-burn acquisition time now, so it's obvious that Apollo 15 has done a burn. We'll continue to stand by live up through the nominal acquisition time. [Pause.] I believe Goldstone has AOS.

a15_0781829.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0781829.text: No. That signal was from the S-IVB Instrument Unit, not from the spacecraft.

a15_0781829.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0781829.text: We're 3 minutes away from the nominal acquisition time now.

a15_0781829.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0781829.text: 10 seconds. AOS on the Command Service Module. We'll allow a little time now for antenna lock up before attempting to talk to the crew but we did get Acquisition Of Signal on time, indicating a good burn.

a15_0785207.speaker: Henize
a15_0785207.text: 15, this is Houston. How do you read?

a15_0785207.speaker: Scott
a15_0785207.text: Oh, this is really profound; I'll tell you, fantastic! [Pause.]

a15_0785207.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0785207.text: First words from Dave Scott in lunar orbit.

a15_0785207.speaker: Scott
a15_0785207.text: Hello, Houston, the Endeavour's on station with cargo, and what a fantastic sight.

a15_0785207.speaker: Scott
a15_0785207.text: And we've got a burn status report for you.

a15_0785207.speaker: Henize
a15_0785207.text: Okay. We're ready to copy whenever you're ready to give it.

a15_0785207.speaker: Scott
a15_0785207.text: Okay. I think our trusty pilot has a first for you on this one. Burn time was 6 plus 38, ignition was on time; the residuals were 0, 0, and 0. Delta V C , minus 4.8; the fuel, 33.25; the oxidizer, 33.3. [Pause.]

a15_0785207.speaker: Henize
a15_0785207.text: That's a beautiful job up there. [Pause.]

a15_0785207.speaker: Scott
a15_0785207.text: And it was a very smooth burn all the way, Karl. There was not a ripple. I guess the only little thing we might comment on was that we had a little PUGS operation after 6 minutes.

a15_0785207.speaker: Scott
a15_0785207.text: And Houston. After our first few minutes of looking here, I don't think we'll have any trouble at all finding new things for you for 6 days.

a15_0785207.speaker: Henize
a15_0785207.text: 15, Houston. We'd like to know the position of the PU valve and also the Unbalance meter reading. [Long pause.]

a15_0785207.speaker: Irwin
a15_0785207.text: The Flow Valve is in Decrease right now. The Unbalance is reading about -25, and I put it in the increase position for about 10 seconds after 6 min - after 6 minutes.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: 15, Houston.

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Houston, 15.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: We've just got through with the [DSE] playback, and we've got excellent burn data down here. And, if you'll give us Accept we'll send up a REFSMMAT.

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Okay; you've got P00 and Accept.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Thank you.

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: And Houston. We're over Mare Crisium at the present time, and the sights are really striking. I guess some of the interesting things we've noted is the variation in albedo from white to dark gray with many variations of gray in between. And many times, this albedo change appears without any significant change in topography, other than perhaps a - a mountain ridge or a chain or a wrinkle ridge or something, but there are many vari - variations in the albedo all over the surface. I guess our general consensus is that it's gray. We haven't noticed any brown yet.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Excellent. If I'm not mistaken, this is probably the first time men have been over Crisium. [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: I guess that's probably right. [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: We have everything from the very old subdued craters that are almost completely washed out to the very bright fresh ones which have interior walls of almost pure white. [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: We're lapping it up down here. Keep talking if you feel like it. [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Another interesting fact that - that we've all noticed is that it - it looks like a great desert across which we've had a number of dust storms. And, in many places, you can see the - the tracks or the swirls across the surface which looks like the - a great dust storm has been blowing across the surface - primarily indicated by the albedo change. But all over Crisium, you can see the streaks, which obviously are from impact at some point or another, but the impression we get is that the [swirls are the] result of a dust storm.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Very interesting. [Pause.] 15. The computer is yours.

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Say again.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: The computer is yours.

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Worden
a15_0791331.text: Karl, this is Al. I'd have to say pretty much what Dave's been saying. You might be interested to know that we're coming up over Peirce right now, and just about to hit the west rim of Mare Crisium, and kind of looking forward to taking a look at Proclus as we get up a little bit closer here. There are a couple of craters just to the north - northeast corner, and we'll pin point those a little better for you later. A very, very small crater that looks like it's had some dark material slide down into the crater, the eastern wall of the inside of the crater has some very dark material in it, and

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Okay; we copy. [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0791331.text: That was Al Worden.

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: And, you know, as we look at all this after the many months we've been studying the Moon, and learning all the technical features and names and everything, why - when you get it all at once, it's just absolutely overwhelming. There are so many different things down there, and such a great variety of land forms and stratigraphy and albedo, that's it's hard for the mental computer to sort it all out and give it back to you. I hope over the next few days we can sort of get our minds organized and get a little more precise on what we're seeing. But I'll tell you; this is absolutely mind-boggling u

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Gentlemen, I can well imagine that a foreign planet must be a weird thing to see.

a15_0791331.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0791331.text: That was Dave Scott.

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: And we've got Proclus in view right now.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Excellent. Tell us about it if you have a chance. [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Well, the - the rays extending from Proclus are very light in color for about [pause] they're very light color for about - oh, 240 to 260 degrees around, and then there's a region of dark mare or albedo. And our - our orientation presently with the spacecraft is such that we have - we're having a tough time figuring out north and south; and, once we get on an orbit track, we'll be able to give you direction a little bit better. But the inner walls of Proclus are very light in color, almost white. The outer walls - the outer ring has a somewhat light gray appearance and the difference in the -

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Beautiful. [Long pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0791331.text: This is Apollo Control. Science commentary on the S-IVB impact will be available in the News Center briefing room. The commentator will be Dave Strangway from the MSC science directorate.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: 15, we would like to have Track to Auto on the High Gain [Antenna]. And, for your information, the Saturn IVB impact is going to take place in just a few minutes. It's going to be a - in a...

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Okay; very good. I wish we were in a...

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Right. It's [in] 2 minutes, 40 seconds, but it's going to be out of your visual range, somewhere around the center area of the Moon. [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Rog. It's too bad we won't get to see it. We'd already taken a look at the map to see if we'd have a chance, but I guess we'll miss that one. [Long pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0791331.text: This is Apollo Control. The seismometer recorders on the monitors in the News Center are giving you a display of the Apollo 14 seismometer - the seismometer on the Apollo 14 ALSEP pack.

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Houston, 15, we're coming up to Serenitatis, and it really looks like an ocean. The landforms, as we approach, are very rugged, very highly cratered, rounded, and we get to the shoreline and we see a few wrinkle ridges that have smoothed out. And we can see, on the far side, on the horizon, the mountains which pick up again on the western side of Serenitatis.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Roger 15.

a15_0791331.speaker: Worden
a15_0791331.text: Okay, Karl. We're coming up over Serenitatis now. We're almost over le Monnier and we can see the Littrow area just out in front of us. And it is, in fact, about three different shades. You can see the - in the upland area, and particularly what looks like down in the valleys, a darker color, and it does look like it's a light powdering - or dusting-over of the entire area. And then, as you get out further into Mare Serenitatis, there's another layering which is a little bit lighter in color. And that - out at the last edge of the wrinkle ridge, out beyond that is the last layer, and the rest

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Roger, Al. Sounds like you're seeing a marvelous amount of detail up there. [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Worden
a15_0791331.text: Well, after - after the King's training, it's almost like I've been here before.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: You can't help yourself, can you.

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: And, Karl. We're approaching the Apennine Mountains, and that is indeed a spectacular view.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Roger...

a15_0791331.speaker: Worden
a15_0791331.text: Sure is, Karl. No question about those mountains being there and where we're at with them.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: They stand up on your horizon, do they? [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Irwin
a15_0791331.text: Yeah; tremendous relief as we approach the mountains, Karl.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Roger. And, for your information, gentlemen, we're getting a good seismic signal from the impact of the Saturn IVB. [Long pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: 15, this is Houston. There is no update required on your T - on your TEI-4 PAD.

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Okay, Houston; understand. Houston, as we cross out of Serenitatis into the Apennines, why, it's just - unreal. You know, those are very poor descriptive terms, but the - mountains jut up out of the 'ocean' here in great relief. I'm sure the guys who've been here before can probably sit down over a cup of coffee and tell you. But the relief is really pervasive.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: You're the first man to fly over this mountain range, Dave. I guess pretty soon you're going to be over the - over the landing site, aren't you?

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Rog, but I'm afraid it'll be dark today.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: That's right. [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Worden
a15_0791331.text: Karl, this is Al again. Looking down into Sulpicius Gallus area, looking at some of the wrinkle ridges and some of the rilles - the arcuate rilles down there, I can make out some distinct color patterns that seem to run parallel to the arcuate rilles - and along the wrinkle ridges, and there is a very subtle darker color, again almost as if it was - some kind of cinder fallout along the ridges and along some of the rilles.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Roger, Al. [Long pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: And Houston; we're coming up here on the terminator and the area, I guess we call Crackled Hills really looks like crackled hills. If you distinguish between the mountains, which are very prominent and smooth, the surface between the first small mountain range and the - what is now the terminator, is relatively flat with a very rough texture - very irregular, lower, crackled hills.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: We copy, Dave. [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Jim's - Jim calls it a gun-metal gray, and that's a - a very good term, I think, for the color that we're seeing now. [Pause.] And as we approach the terminator, of course, the relief stands out even more. The shadows are getting much longer, and the peaks of the mountains, as they're silhouetted against the - the Crackled Hills, seem to have a - a diffuse shadow at the top. The shadow, as it goes from the base of the mountain to it's peak, is very sharp. And around the top of the mountain, it becomes more diffuse, not - not quite as sharp and begins to blend in with the - the surface on which

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Roger, Dave. Sounds very interesting.

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Houston, we're trying to get oriented here so we can perhaps pick out some of the features near the landing site. There's quite a bit of shadow now, but we have Aristillus and Autolycus very clearly. And with the low sun angle, the surface between those two large craters and the rim of Imbrium - the eastern rim of Imbrium is very rough, quite a bit of debris, and it looks like it probably came out of the two craters. I believe we can see Hadley C, just barely in the shadows.

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Roger, 15. We copy that. Did I understand that the rim of Autolycus is standing up in the sunlight?

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Yes, that's true. Aristillus and Autolycus both have their eastern rims exposed to the sunlight and we get a pretty good look at the elevation on the rim. And Autolycus, to it's north eastern side, seems to have a - a saddle or somewhat depressed rim. And as you come around to the west - or the eastern side of Aristillus, it seems to be relatively level or horizontal, with a few subtle saddles and depressions. Autolycus appears to have a - a relatively horizontal or - or even rim all the way around, and we can see sunlight on the northwestern side of Autolycus, on the rim, just barely a tick o

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Roger. It sounds like a fantastic view. [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Worden
a15_0791331.text: It really is. [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Gordon
a15_0791331.text: [Do] you guys have enough to keep you busy for a few days then?

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Hey, Dick, we've got enough to keep us busy for months, and months, and months, as you well know. [Long pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: The outer rims of Aristillus and Autolycus seem to be quite heavily cratered and rough; and Aristillus, on it's east-northeastern side, seems to have a couple of benches on the outer rim as it goes down to the surface, and their - the shadows are - are exposed quite well. [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Gordon
a15_0791331.text: Roger, Dave. [Long pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Houston, just north of Conon, there's a - a great depression in the mountains - a low part of the mountains. In the - The western side of the mountains is exposed to the sunlight, and this reflects back in to the shadowed part of the mountains which - the base - basin, just north of Conon there, is really shadowed by the eastern mountain range; but the reflectivity back from the - the mountains exposed to the sunlight illuminates the - the shadowed area to [the point] where we can pick out craters and ridges and various other topographic features [in the dark]. It's - its really quite interest

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Roger. That sounds like a fascinating illumination. Do you - do you have any inclination that you're going to be able to see the dark side of Moon with Earthlight on it? [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Well, we can just barely see subtle features now, I think. We can see the horizon quite clearly. [Pause.]

a15_0791331.speaker: Henize
a15_0791331.text: Roger. When you get dark-adapted, it may be that things will come through pretty well.

a15_0791331.speaker: Scott
a15_0791331.text: Rog.

a15_0791331.speaker: Mission Control
a15_0791331.text: This is Apollo Control. The Flight Dynamics Officer [FIDO], Bill Boone, reports that after tracking from Acquisition Of Signal, the orbital parameters are 169 [over the near-side] by 59 nautical miles [over the far-side] [313 by 109.3 km].

a15_0794827.speaker: Henize
a15_0794827.text: Jim, the people down here would appreciate it if you could give them something of a description of the operation of the PU valve during the LOI burn. [Pause.]

a15_0794827.speaker: Irwin
a15_0794827.text: Roger, Karl. There was no operation of the - the PU valve at all until crossover. And then at crossover, it required a - a Decrease, and then at about - about 5 minutes and a half into the burn, it started to increase, and I went to the - the Increase position at that time. All the operation of the PUGS manual operation occurred after crossover.

a15_0794827.speaker: Irwin
a15_0794827.text: And, as I mentioned, about 5 and a half, I went to - 5 and a half minutes, I went - went to neutral and then the - it looked like the Unbalance was going to go - it was rapidly departing the zero region, and that was about the time we went through 6 minutes, and I put it into minimum at that time - into the Decrease position.

a15_0794827.speaker: Henize
a15_0794827.text: Okay, Jim. That answered our next question. [Long pause.]

a15_0794827.speaker: Henize
a15_0794827.text: And, 15, the people down here were very much turned on by your description of the swirls on the floor of Crisium. We trust you got some good photography of that; and, if you didn't, they'd very much appreciate having some next time around.

a15_0794827.speaker: Scott
a15_0794827.text: Okay. We were discussing our photography, and we're going to try and stay as close to the preplanned photos as we can and not over extend ourselves into what's already planned for the six days.
