a15a1045755.text: Roger. Houston...

a15a1045755.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1045755.text: ...Pan camera Pad is the same.

a15a1045755.speaker: Worden
a15a1045755.text: Okay, Houston. Understand mapping camera and pan camera Pads are the same. T-start, 105:52:58 and T-stop 106:17:57.

a15a1045755.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1045755.text: That's correct. Your Rev 16 map camera Pad...(Pause while he gets an instruction from the Flight Director) Endeavour, Houston, give us P00 (Program Zero-Zero) and Accept, and we'll up-link while we're talking here. [Scott - "Program Zero-Zero was pronounced 'Pooh', after (A.A. Milne's) Winnie the Pooh."] [With the computer in P00 and Accept, Houston can directly load revised state vectors - spacecraft positions and velocities - and other data.]

a15a1045755.speaker: Worden
a15a1045755.text: Okay. You've got Accept, and I'm in a middle of a maneuver (that is, a spacecraft re-orientation) right now.

a15a1045755.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1045755.text: Okay. Leave it in P20 .

a15a1045755.speaker: Worden
a15a1045755.text: Okay.

a15a1045755.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1045755.text: And your T-start 106...

a15a1045755.speaker: Worden
a15a1045755.text: Go ahead with rev 16.

a15a1045755.speaker: Worden
a15a1045755.text: Understand. T-start, 106:56:51. T-stop, 108:55:19.

a15a1045755.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1045755.text: That's a good readback, Al. (Long Pause) Endeavour, Houston. If you'll give us an Enter, we can go ahead with the load.

a15a1045755.speaker: Worden
a15a1045755.text: Okay. (Long Pause) [The NASA Public Affairs commentator tells the press that a preliminary estimate of where Dave landed, based on LM guidance system data, is 1900 feet (570 meters) south of target. The LM is actually about 625 meters NNW of the target.]

a15a1045755.speaker: Irwin
a15a1045755.text: Houston, are you copying the AGS Cal(ibration) values?

a15a1045755.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1045755.text: That's affirm, Falcon. [Comm Break. The Abort Guidance System Calibration procedures are on Surface 1.2.]

a15a1045755.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1045755.text: Endeavour, Houston. The computer's yours.

a15a1045755.speaker: Worden
a15a1045755.text: Roger; Houston. (Pause) [Here, Mitchell is telling Al that the uplink has been completed and that he can switch out of P00.]

a15a1045755.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1045755.text: Endeavour and Falcon, Houston. Could I talk with (you) a minute? (Pause)

a15a1045755.speaker: Worden
a15a1045755.text: Houston, this is Endeavour. Go ahead.

a15a1045755.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1045755.text: And Falcon, Houston. (Pause)

a15a1045755.speaker: Scott
a15a1045755.text: Go ahead, Houston, Hadley Base here. [Scott - "You notice, there, we went from Falcon to Hadley Base. That was by design. 'Cause we decided, once we're on the ground, it was no longer a flying machine, it is not the Falcon. It has changed into a base. And then it will fly again. Probably you've discussed the many roles of the Lunar Module with the other guys. It was a marvelous piece of machine with so many features built in. It was so many different things. Which is pretty remarkable when somebody started with a plain piece of paper. It's home now, and a laboratory, and all those other things

a15a1045755.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1045755.text: Okay, crew. The President sends his regards through (NASA Administrator) Dr. (James) Fletcher, and I read: "The President sends his congratulations to the entire ground team and the Apollo 15 crew on a successful landing and sends his best wishes for the rest of the mission."

a15a1045755.speaker: Scott
a15a1045755.text: Rog; Houston. Thank you. Our appreciation...

a15a1045755.speaker: Worden
a15a1045755.text: Houston, this is Endeavour. Thank you very much.

a15a1045755.speaker: Scott
a15a1045755.text: ...to the President, and I'd like to thank you, too, for the support we've had.

a15a1045755.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1045755.text: Roger. Roger. (Pause)

a15a1045755.speaker: Scott
a15a1045755.text: And, Houston, the Hadley Base here. Tell those geologists in the Backroom to get ready because we've really got something for them.

a15a1045755.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1045755.text: Which group of guys in the back room? [Comm Break] [Flight controllers in the Mission Operation Control Room (MOCR) were supported by teams of experts working in support rooms scattered around the Johnson Space Center and at various off-site contractor facilities. The science support team occupied one of these so-called backrooms. Because the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal concentrates on the EVAs, when we refer to the capitalized Backroom, we are always talking about the team in the science support room. Dave's remark at 105:08:16 indicates that, at this point in the mission, he is also thinkin

a15a1051056.speaker: Worden
a15a1051056.text: Okay Ed. If you've got the gyro torquing angles, I'll torque them out on the minute.

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Roger. We copied (the angles).

a15a1051056.speaker: Worden
a15a1051056.text: Okay, Houston; Endeavour. I'll wait until the even minute to torque them out.

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Roger. On the even minute. (Pause) Falcon, Houston. Stand by on your stars, and let us give you some new ones. 105:11:33 Scott: Okay. Standing by. [Because of the LM tilt, the stars listed on Surface 1-5 are not the ideal ones to use for the platform alignment.] [Scott - "As you know, we had 36 stars that we learned and used as navigation stars. On Apollo 9, we did a lot of star work. I'd been working on the G&N (Guidance and Navigation), so the sextant and the star catalog were part of my early responsibilities (in Gemini). So, when we got to go on Apollo 9, and started finalizing what we wer

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Okay. The first pair, we will have star 3 (Navi) in detent 3 ; star 12 (Rigel) in detent 6. Second pair...

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: 3 in detent 3 and 12 in detent 6. [ Star 3 is Gamma Cassiopeiae (Navi) in the constellation Cassiopeia and star 12 is Beta Orionis (Rigel) in Orion.]

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: That's affirm. Second pair, we'll have star 61 - that's Epsilon Orionis - in detent 6. Then Noun 88 , plus 10975, plus 99373, minus 02127. Star 122, Schedar, is your second (and will be) in detent 3. Noun 88, plus 54566, plus 09353, plus 83277. And if you're questioning, there weren't any other nav star pairs available, apparently.

a15a1051056.speaker: Irwin
a15a1051056.text: Okay, Ed. I understand. For the first P57 , it's 3 in detent 3 and 12 in detent 6. And then for the second pair, it's star 61 in detent 6, and the Noun 88 values are plus 10975, plus 99373, minus 02127. And then star 122, in detent 3; plus 54566, plus 09353, and plus 83277.

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: That's a good readback, Jim. (Long Pause) [Jones - "Now, the numbers Ed read up were star coordinates so that you could use the AOT (Alignment Optical Telescope) and check to see that the stars were where they were supposed to be and fine tune the platform alignment."] [Scott - "Yeah. Or you could drive the AOT to the stars with the computer. You could enter it into the computer so you would align your platform based on the stars, and you'd be ready to go. And then we put everything to sleep and then woke it up again for the take-off. Let's see. There were some other things we could do with th

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Falcon, Houston. Your vent's complete. You can terminate.

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: Roger. Thank you. [Long Comm Break] [During this Comm Break, Ed Mitchell reminds the Flight Director that the Command Module is about to go behind the Moon and asks if there is any unfinished business that needs to be conducted prior to LOS (Loss-of-Signal). The Flight Director conducts a poll and finds that there is none.]

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Endeavour, Houston. 1 minute until LOS. You're looking good from here. (Long Pause) Endeavour, Houston. 30 seconds to LOS. Do you read?

a15a1051056.speaker: Worden
a15a1051056.text: Houston, Endeavour. Rog.

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: And you look good from the ground, Al. We'll see you on the other side.

a15a1051056.speaker: Worden
a15a1051056.text: Okay, Ed. [Comm Break. Dave and Jim are finishing their first pair of stars.]

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Falcon, we copy your Noun 93 . [O'Brien - "Once the stars have been sighted through the AOT, Noun 93 displays the angular distance that the platform must be moved to bring it back into correct alignment."]

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: Okay; we'll torque them at 22:30.

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Stand by one.

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: Standing by.

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Okay; proceed with your torquing.

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: On the way. (Pause) Okay, Houston. Standing by on the RLS (Reference Landing Site).

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Stand by one.

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: Okay. (Pause)

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Okay; let's reject those, Dave.

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: All right, reject. [Comm Break] [The torquing angles are changes in the platform alignment derived from the sightings on the first pair of stars. Houston has decided that those angles don't make sense. Dave and Jim will now proceed to the sightings with the second pair of stars.] [In Houston, the Flight Director is told that Dave and Jim have incorrectly loaded the final digit of Noun 88 into the computer. Mitchell notes that the mistake can be caught when the numbers are re-loaded.]

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Falcon, Houston. When the Noun 88 (the star coordinates) comes up again, hold it, please.

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: Okay, Houston. I didn't copy the name of the star, but how about Castor or Pollux or Betelgeuse or somebody like that?

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Okay; stand by. We'll tell you which one it is; we think it's in the middle of the belt (in the constellation of Orion), Dave.

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: Which one, Jim?

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: Alnilam! Alnilam! Yeah, we got that.

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Rog; it's the middle star.

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: Sure, old (playing with syllables) Aludiman!

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: You're right. (Pause)

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: It's nice to see friends. (Pause) [Scott - "There's a story about that one. But I don't remember the story. But we knew him well. Names of stars mean a lot more than numbers. I remember one star that we used near the Big Dipper, the name of which I can't recall, but there's a star in the Big Dipper, near one of the stars that we used, which was the north star at the time the pyramids were built. It is no longer the north star. Many people forget that things in the heavens change over time, and the things that were there when the pyramids were built are different from the things that are there

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: Okay, Houston. We can use this one, but we don't have the Noun 88 for it.

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Yes, you do. That's what we gave you, Dave.

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: Okay; we'll try it again. (Long Pause)

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: Houston, why don't you read us the Noun 88s again then, please?

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Roger. Plus 10975. (Pause)

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: Go.

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Plus 99373. (Pause)

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: Go.

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Minus 02127.

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: Okay; that's exactly what we just loaded. We'll see where it takes us.

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: We're seeing it...On the last register, we're seeing a minus 02124.

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: Sure, that's just a round-off.

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Yeah, you're probably right. [Scott - "What I'm doing is loading the coordinates into the computer to drive the AOT so that it lines up with a star. And you look in the AOT and see the star and you know that everything's where it's supposed to be. You notice a little deviation from normal procedure where he reads up the numbers instead of me reading the numbers back to him? Instead of copying them, I was just punching them into the computer directly."] [Jones - "And they could look and see what was in the registers."] [Scott - "Yeah. And then he called up and said 'Hey, we see a different numb

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: And...Let's take a look at the Noun 79 , and that's not even close. [O'Brien - "Dave is having difficulty locating star 61, Epsilon Orionis, in the AOT. Noun 79 displays the AOT coordinates of the star, but unfortunately, Houston has given him the wrong coordinates."]

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Okay. (Pause) Dave, we specified it for detent 6, and the computer's giving you detent 5.

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: I should have noticed that, Ed; I'm sorry. (Long Pause) [Scott - "There was a knob on the telescope that you rotated to put it in the detents."] [Jones - "So it was a mechanical change rather than a computer change."] [Scott - "Each of the six detents would point to a different 60-degree field-of-view in the hemisphere above the LM. There was no mechanical articulation (capability of movement) within a detent other than rotating the cursor and spiral. The computer numbers for a star within the field-of-view of a particular detent were unique."]

a15a1051056.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1051056.text: Okay, Dave, the spiral should be about 330 and the cursor about 148, if that helps.

a15a1051056.speaker: Scott
a15a1051056.text: (That's) right on. [Long Comm Break] [Dave's 'right on' means that the cursor and spiral readings Ed gave him are exactly what he is seeing in the AOT.] MP3 Audio Clip ( 13 min 36 sec ) by David Shaffer

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: Falcon, Houston.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Go.

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: If you'd like some help being coached on to this next star, it's in (the constellation) Cassiopeia, and we're suggesting detent 3. (It should) be a spiral of 181, a cursor of 23, and it should be just to the left of Navi, the bright star to the left of Navi.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Okay.

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: And we'll give you the Noun 88s when you get to them.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Oh yeah, Schedar. Rog.

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: That's affirm.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Okay. (Pause) Okay; we'll cycle back, Ed. (Long Pause)

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: Okay, Falcon; Houston. (We) observed your cycle back. We'll to have to rerun that first star again.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Yes; Rog, Ed. The reason I did that was because we need to stick an erasable load in here on the Noun 79 . [Comm Break]

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Okay, Houston. It doesn't look like the program is running exactly right.

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: What seems to be the problem, Dave? It looks good from here.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: (Sounding a bit doubtful) Okay, we'll try; but we're in a loop here where it won't accept detent 6, I believe; but we'll press on.

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: It's always going to give the first one it computes, Dave. (Pause) Change it to (detent) 6 and go ahead. [Comm Break]

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: Okay, Dave, you ready for your second Noun 88s ?

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Well, I think we've got them on board if that's what you read us.

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: Rog. You're going great; keep going. (Long Pause)

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Okay, Ed; I have Schedar.

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: Very good, Dave. [Comm Break. They are doing the second star sighting and, in the next exchange with Houston, are at the bottom of checklist page Surface 1-5.] [Scott, from the 1971 Technical Debrief - "The (platform) alignment was straightforward once we got the (Noun) 88 procedures squared away...The new procedures developed by MIT to perform P57's was very good and save quite a bit of time. We had an extra pad (that is, a time cushion) in there based on the old techniques of having to cursor and then spiral. Now that you can go straight through, it saves quite a bit of time and it's a valua

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Okay, Houston; the torquing angles are up.

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: Roger. Stand by. (Long Pause) Okay, Pro(ceed).

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Okay; they're in. (Pause) And how about the RLS (Reference Landing Site)? Do you want to take it?

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: Negative, Falcon.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Roger on the negative.

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: Okay, Falcon; Houston. We need to redesignate the rendezvous radar to 180, 270, 00 for thermal protection.

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: That's affirm. (Long Pause) [Jones - "I think you're parking the rendezvous radar ( LM-9 photo by Randy Attwood) so that it doesn't heat up. It was up on top of the LM, but you could park it to minimize the cross-section to the Sun. Is that right?"] [Scott - "Thermal considerations were always important. The environment of the Moon is different from the environment of the Earth, and thermal considerations are quite different."] [Jones - "You don't have convective heating or cooling."] [Scott - "Yeah, that's the atmosphere that provides that here on Earth. But the difference in the heat, the te

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: And, Falcon; Houston. As soon as you get the radar parked, we're ready for the E-Mod dump.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Roger. [Comm Break. In E-Mod dump they will download the entire contents of the computer memory to Houston. This item is at the top of Surface 1-6.] [Jones - "Could they read the whole memory?"] [Scott - "They could read the same thing we read."] [Jones - "That is, they could read the display."] [Scott - "They had the same numbers we had. When I say 'the torquing angles are up' I've got them on the DSKY and they've got them on their DSKY."] [Jones - "For them to look at the whole memory, you'd have to do a E(rasable)-memory dump?"] [Scott - "I don't remember, exactly, but they could see practi

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Okay, Houston; here comes your E-Mod dump.

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: Roger; ready. (Pause)

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: And, Houston, (as per checklist page Surface 1-6) we'll be standing by for your Stay NoStay.

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: And, Roger, you have a Stay.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Got a Stay; thank you. (Long Pause) [Journal Contributor Harald Kucharek notes that, in his book Failure is not an Option , Gene Kranz says that 'Stay NoStay' originates with Howard Tindall in one instance from the legendary series of Tindallgrams: "Once we get to the Moon, does Go mean 'stay' on the surface, and does NoGo mean abort from the surface? I think the Go NoGo decision should be changed to Stay NoStay or something like this." Tindall can be seen standing, third from the left, next to Deke Slayton, in Apollo 13 photo S70-35013 .]

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: And, Falcon; Houston. We're going to delete the 10-minute delay, so you can go right into P06 and power down.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Roger. [Comm Break. NASA's Public Affairs commentator mentions to the press that, because of the problems they had with the star sightings, they are a little behind the timeline. As indicated on checklist page Surface 1-6, they had planned to wait ten minutes after performing the E-Mod dump before opening the IMU (Inertial Measurements Unit, the inertial platform) circuit breaker and, thereby, power it down. They will, instead, perform an immediate powerdown.] [Irwin, from the 1971 Technical Debrief - "There was a little bit of confusion on the P57 , using two Noun 88 stars. That held us up a

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: And, Houston; 15. ED batteries both check at 37.

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: Roger; Roger. ED Batts. [Long Comm Break]

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: And, Falcon; Houston. We're having changeover (of flight control teams) down here; didn't get a chance to say "real good job" on that descent.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Okay; thank you, Ed. And (we) appreciate all your help, too. The comm was super today, and everybody back there was right on top of it all the way. We sure appreciate that help.

a15a1053410.speaker: Mitchell
a15a1053410.text: And looked real good from here, Dave. We'll see you on lift-off.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Okay, thanks Ed-o. (Long Pause) [Astronaut Joe Allen takes over as CapCom. The new Flight Director is Milton Windler, who is taking over from Glynn Lunney.]

a15a1053410.speaker: Allen
a15a1053410.text: Hello, Falcon; this is Houston.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Hello there, Houston; how are you?

a15a1053410.speaker: Allen
a15a1053410.text: Super down here, Dave and Jim. From what I heard, it was not only a good landing, it was a great landing. And it sounds like you didn't even bend anything. [Jones - "Is this a reference to the longer engine bell?"] [Scott - "Probably. That had been discussed. But, at this point, we don't know that yet because we haven't looked at it."] [Jones - "A dry wit."] [Scott - "Oh, yes. Joe's got a very dry wit. He's very quick."]

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Well, I hope not, Joe. But we're sure in a fine place here. We can see St. George (Crater); it looks like it's right over a little rise. I'm sure it's much farther than that. We can see Bennett Hill . We see something off at our, like, 1 o'clock that's a pretty good elevation. We're not too sure of that, but we'll give you some more detail later on.

a15a1053410.speaker: Allen
a15a1053410.text: Roger. We're standing by. [Comm Break] [Clock positions are given relative to the forward, west-facing windows. 12 o'clock is west; 3 o'clock is north; and so on. Bennett Hill is named for trajectory designer Floyd Bennett .]

a15a1053410.speaker: Allen
a15a1053410.text: Falcon, Houston.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Go, Houston.

a15a1053410.speaker: Allen
a15a1053410.text: Dave, we've got some vital questions down here. First, did you see the rille on the way down?

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: (Guffawing) Sure, Joe. Easy.

a15a1053410.speaker: Allen
a15a1053410.text: Roger. And did you read the VHF call from Endeavour right shortly before the landing?

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Negative.

a15a1053410.speaker: Allen
a15a1053410.text: Roger.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Why? Did he have something to say?

a15a1053410.speaker: Allen
a15a1053410.text: I'm sure he did, Dave; but we're wondering if you ever heard him call you on VHF. It sounds like we're going to have to do a VHF comm check.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: No, we tried that comm check 3 minutes prior to PDI and we got no response. And Houston verified that the Endeavour could hear us, but we did not hear him. [O'Brien - "In the Apollo 15 Mission Report , the cause of Falcon's failure to receive Endeavour was attributed to a simple checklist error. In the checklists, the Command Module was transmitting on 296.8 MHz, but the Lunar Module was receiving on 259.7 MHz."]

a15a1053410.speaker: Allen
a15a1053410.text: Roger. We copy. And we have Rev 16 through 20 lift-off times when you're ready.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Okay; give us 5 minutes to clean up the cockpit here. (Pause)

a15a1053410.speaker: Allen
a15a1053410.text: Roger, Dave. We're standing by. (Pause) And be advised the Backroom's doing slow rolls just from your first description there.

a15a1053410.speaker: Scott
a15a1053410.text: Okay, we've got a lot more coming. Stand by. [Comm Break] [The "Back Room" is the Science Support Room. Dave and Jim are probably reconfiguring switches and circuit breakers as indicated on checklist pages Surface 1-7 through 1-11. The NASA Public Affairs commentator tells the press that the current best estimate of the LM location is 300 feet north and 300 feet east of the planned landing site. They are getting closer.] [Jones - "Could you help me understand the importance of the VHF comm check?"] [Scott - "As I recall, there were two things the VHF did. It gave you a direct voice link betwee

a15a1053410.speaker: Irwin
a15a1053410.text: Okay, Joe; this is Jim. I'm standing by to copy some lift-off data.

a15a1053410.speaker: Allen
a15a1053410.text: Roger, Jim. Lift-off time for T-16, 108:39:45; T-17, 110:38:00; T-18, 112:36:13; T-19, 114:34:26; and T-20, 116:32:39. Over. [T-16 refers to the 16th orbit of the Moon by the Command Module.]

a15a1053410.speaker: Allen
a15a1053410.text: Roger, Jim. Readback's correct. Sounds good. [Long Comm Break] Landing at Hadley Apollo 15 Journal Preparations for the Stand-up EVA

a15_1060740csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1060740csm.text: Hello, Houston. Hello, Houston. This is Endeavour.

a15_1060740csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1060740csm.text: Roger. [We've] had a CapCom shift [change] here, Al, and you're coming up on a change from - to Mono on the Pan Camera. I'll let you get that, in about...

a15_1060740csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1060740csm.text: ...20 seconds. Endeavour, Houston. In 15 seconds, you need to change the Pan Camera to Mono. Just a reminder.

a15_1060740csm.speaker: Mission Control
a15_1060740csm.text: CapCom Gordon Fullerton is at the moment conversing with Al Worden, aboard the Command Module Endeavour , which has its scientific instruments in operation in the SIM bay at this time; both cameras and the Gamma-ray [Spectrometer] and Laser Altimeter.

a15_1060740csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1060740csm.text: And, Al, when you're ready, I have a P24 PAD, the LM visual, and also a couple of changes to the Flight Plan. Over.

a15_1060740csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1060740csm.text: Okay. I'm all set up and ready to copy.

a15_1060740csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1060740csm.text: Okay. P24 landmark track PAD, LM visual. T-1 is 106:33:59; T-2 is 106:38:06; TCA is 106:40:29; T-3 106:40:57; you're off-track three nautical miles north. And one note on that, use Omni Charlie. Over. [Pause.]

a15_1060740csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1060740csm.text: Roger. Copy. P24 PAD. T-1, starting with the times, T-1, 106:33:59; 38:06; 40:29; 40:57; off-track north, three miles, and use Omni Charlie.

a15_1060740csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1060740csm.text: Okay; readback's correct. And [there's a Flight Plan] change at 106:45. Let me know when you're there.

a15_1060740csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1060740csm.text: You say you have a change at 106:45?

a15_1060740csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1060740csm.text: That's affirmative, Al. Change where it says "Gamma-ray, Gain Step, Shield, Off." Change that to read "Gamma-ray: Gain Step, increase one step." Over.

a15_1060740csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1060740csm.text: Understand, Gordo. It says "Gamma-ray, Gain Step, increase one step" at that time.

a15_1060740csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1060740csm.text: That's affirmative. Then at 106:56, delete the "Gain Step, Shield, On" remark there, and the reason is to adjust the spectrum. Over.

a15a1061105.speaker: Worden
a15a1061105.text: Rog; understand. You want that whole line deleted at - at 106:56, then.

a15a1061105.speaker: Scott
a15a1061105.text: Say, I think we need a couple of words on the PLSS stowed on the cabin floor. We've got the two pins out on the side and can't seem to get it up. Do you have any good words on that?

a15a1061105.speaker: Scott
a15a1061105.text: Okay. [Comm Break] [Jim's PLSS is stowed on the floor between them, in front of the hatch, and is held in place by removable pins. Dave's PLSS is stowed at his left shoulder on the cabin wall. They are in the middle of the left-hand column of Surface 2-1, preparing for the Stand-up EVA or SEVA. They will not be wearing the PLSSs for the SEVA but, rather, will remain hooked up to the LM ECS (Environmental Control System). They are merely getting Jim's PLSS out of the way.]

a15a1061105.speaker: Allen
a15a1061105.text: Rog; Dave. We suggest you try, first, holding the bracket at the front, in place, while you push the PLSS aft and jiggle it.

a15a1061105.speaker: Scott
a15a1061105.text: Okay. [Comm Break] MP3 Audio Clip ( 9 min 24 sec ) by David Shaffer

a15_1061439csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1061439csm.text: Endeavour, Houston. Reminder, Pan Camera, Stereo, at 14:58.

a15a1061616.speaker: Allen
a15a1061616.text: Falcon, Houston. Any luck with the PLSS?

a15a1061616.speaker: Scott
a15a1061616.text: Oh, Rog. Sorry. Yes. We got it up; that worked fine. (Long Pause) [Scott - "If you have a problem, the easiest thing to do is to tell the guys in Houston, because they have this army of people who are addressing problems. Rather than fuss with something and try and solve it yourself, it was a lot easier and more effective to say, 'Hey Joe, I got a little problem.' Then, we could go on and do something else, knowing full well that the army back there would go work the problem."] [Jones - "And the one guy or the two guys who really knew about that stuff and had designed it and fussed with it..."

a15a1061616.speaker: Allen
a15a1061616.text: And, Dave, we thought the transmission time between Earth and Moon was unusually long there.

a15a1061616.speaker: Scott
a15a1061616.text: It sort of was. [Long Comm Break] [Scott - "Because I didn't tell them we got it fixed, the guy who passed up the instructions way back there in a backroom somewhere is sitting there saying 'Well, what happened!?' And of course, on board, we got it up, it's working fine, so we pressed on, and forgot to tell them that it worked."] [Jones - "There was a lot more going on in the spacecraft than what we hear here."] [Scott - "There was a lot more going on in the world. Everywhere. The voice tape is brief, skimpy, incomplete, but continuous."] [Jones - "And it's a hook to hang a lot of other stuff

a15_1061737csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1061737csm.text: Endeavour, Houston. 20 seconds to your camera T-stop time.

a15_1061737csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1061737csm.text: Endeavour, Houston. We're ver - we verify that the lens is tucked in. You're clear to turn the Pan Camera, Off.

a15_1061737csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1061737csm.text: Hadley Base, this is Houston. (Long Pause)

a15_1061737csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1061737csm.text: Go ahead there, Joe; this is Hadley Base.

a15_1061737csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1061737csm.text: Dave and Jim, while you're working there, thought you'd be interested in the report that the SIM bay is giving us some remarkable data. It seems to be working beautifully.

a15_1061737csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1061737csm.text: Good; we're hoping we can compete with it. [Very Long Comm Break. The SIM bay is the Scientific Equipment Module on the Command Module. During this Comm Break, Dave and Jim are preparing the equipment they will need or the Stand-up EVA, getting the cameras ready, getting out the Lunar Extravehicular Visor Assemblies (LEVAs), applying an anti-fogging agent to the inside of their bubble helmets, etc. Dave's next transmission indicates that they are now at the top of Surface 2-2. ]

a15_1062638csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1062638csm.text: Endeavour, Houston. If you read, Omni Charlie.

a15_1063158csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1063158csm.text: Endeavour, Houston. Endeavour, Houston. Give us Omni Charlie, if you read.

a15_1063158csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063158csm.text: Okay, Houston; Hadley base on VOX (voice-activated comm). How do you read?

a15_1063158csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1063158csm.text: Okay, Dave; you're loud and clear.

a15_1063158csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063158csm.text: Joe, how do you read me?

a15_1063158csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1063158csm.text: Five by (five), Jim; sounds great. ["Five by five" means "loud and clear".]

a15_1063158csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063158csm.text: Okay, we're configured; we're down to helmet and glove donning, and...(Long Pause)

a15_1063158csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063158csm.text: (Connecting the LM oxygen hoses, which they had taken off after the landing) Okay; red to red and blue to...(Pause) Position mikes; don the helmets. (Pause)

a15_1063158csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063158csm.text: (Because of the left-rearward LM tilt) I keep sliding to your side for some reason.

a15_1063158csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063158csm.text: While I was in the LM (means the CSM, possibly), it was the other way around; I was sliding to the right. (Long Pause) Okay, don the helmets and don the LEVAs (Lunar Extravehicular Visor Assembly) Get yours first as per usu(ual). [The LEVA is the balaclava-like assembly that covers the clear bubble helmet. The LEVA provides thermal protection and contains a set of visors and sunshields that can be raised and lowered as needed while the astronauts are working outside.]

a15_1063158csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1063158csm.text: Roger, Dave and Jim; we copy. And just as a reminder, we're starting to bite into the sleep period a little bit.

a15_1063158csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063158csm.text: Okay; understand. (Pause) [Scott - "The clock is running faster than it did in training! Have you ever discussed with the other guys the fact that time during flight seems to go more quickly than the time in simulations, and the reasons for that? The history behind some of that? As an example, when the guys at Edwards used to fly the X-15, they ran their simulations in fast time, in that they would run six tenths of a second in the simulator for each second of flight time. Because you find out that, in flight, things take you longer and, therefore, time seems to go more quickly. And, one reaso

a15_1063158csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063158csm.text: Okay; your helmet's locked. [The click of Jim's helmet lock is audible.]

a15_1063158csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063158csm.text: Okay, (garbled) locked. (Long Pause as Jim helps Dave get his helmet and LEVA on and locked)

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1063500csm.text: Endeavour, Houston. If you read, go Omni Charlie. [Pause.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1063500csm.text: Hello, Houston; Endeavour. On Omni Charlie now.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay, Al. Loud and clear, and you're just about to T-1. I guessed you just passed it.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay, Gordo. And I've been reading you right along.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Tight today, aren't they? [Because they have not yet started glove-donning, this is probably a reference to Dave's helmet lock, the lock-lock described below or the LEVA straps. Three suits were made for each crew member: a training suit, which got well broken in during the long months of training leading up to the mission, a flight suit, and a backup. At this point in the mission, the flight suits are virtually brand-new.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: They are. (Long Pause) Okay.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1063500csm.text: Endeavour, Houston. We're getting kind of a weak signal. Would you go to best Omni. [Pause.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay; verify the following: (reading) helmet and visors aligned and adjusted. Yours are. Let me check your O2. Okay; red one's lock-lock; blue, lock-lock; the gas connectors both in a lock-lock. [The helmet lock and connector locks are ring locks which, as a backup, have devices called lock-locks which hold the ring locks in place. The lock-locks are operated by squeezing a pair of tabs with thumb and forefinger and sliding them in or out of the locked position. Operating the lock-locks with gloves on is not a trivial task. This is one of the several reasons that the gloves are donned last.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1063500csm.text: Roger, Gordo. Going best. [Long pause.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: Let me check yours. (Pause) Okay; yours are okay.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay; PGA diverter valves to horizontal?

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay, Houston; Endeavour. Looks like Omni Charlie's it.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: Mine's verified. [With the PGA diverter valve in the horizontal position, all of the air flow entering the suit comes in at the neck ring. With the valve in the vertical position, some of the flow would enter in the torso.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay, don EV (extravehicular) gloves. (Long Pause)

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1063500csm.text: Roger. Understand you're on Omni Charlie. [Long pause.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1063500csm.text: Endeavour, Houston. We can't get a - a data with you. We'd like you to put the DSE to Low Bit Rate, Record, Forward, and Command Reset.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay. Understand you want Low Bit Rate, Record, Forward and Reset.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1063500csm.text: That's affirmative, Al.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay, my gloves are on. [Several of the astronauts - Jack Schmitt, in particular - had trouble donning the gloves. The 15 crew is impressively fast.] [Scott - "In the training sessions on this, we did exactly this: we read every word all the time. So it becomes automatic when you get there. A lot of times people would think that, if you read it so much - and this happens sometimes in airplanes - it becomes meaningless. One reason it takes you so long up there is because it's not meaningless, because, now, you're really paying attention. This is a rehearsal we practiced in the mission simulator

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: All right. My gloves are on. Let me check yours. (Pause) Okay, locked and locked. Check mine.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay, Gordo. You got it.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1063500csm.text: Roger. I think we're getting a little better comm now. [Long pause.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay, you're locked.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay. [In the following sequence, they will reconfigure the ECS (Environmental Control System) Suit Circuit in preparation for the cabin depressurization. Readers interested in a detailed description of the ECS and the Suit Circuit should consult the Apollo Operations Handbook.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: Pressure integrity check. Okay, if you'll read to me. [The ECS controls are behind Jim who, undoubtedly, has turned around to reach them.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay. Suit Gas Diverter (Valve) , Pull-Egress; verify.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: Verified. [They have verified that there is no air flow from the ECS into the cabin.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Cabin Gas Return (Valve) , Egress; verify?

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: Verified. [Here, they are verifying that there is no flow from the cabin back into the ECS .]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Suit Circuit Relief (Valve), Close?

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: Close. [The Suit Circuit Relief valve would normally open if the pressure in the circuit exceeded 5.3 pounds per square inch (psi). Here, they are making sure that the relief valve will not open during the SEVA.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Press Reg(ulator) A to Egress?

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: A to Egress. [In the Cabin position, one or both of the two Pressure Demand Regulators would maintain the cabin pressure in the range of 4.6 to 5.0 psi. In the Egress position, enough oxygen is added to the Suit Circuit to maintain the Suit Circuit pressure in the range 3.6 to 4.0 psi.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Press Reg B , Direct O2?

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: Direct O2. [With Reg B in Direct O2, there will be an unregulated flow of oxygen into the suit circuit, albeit at a modest flow rate of 7 pounds per hour. This flow is enough to pressurize the heretofore unpressurized suits. Now, they will monitor the suit pressurization and, once the suits are pressurized to 3.7 psi above cabin pressure, they will shut of the oxygen flow and monitor the suits to make sure there are no leaks. Once they are satisfied with the suit integrity, then they will depressurize the cabin.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay, (reading) monitor cuff gauge to 3.7 to 4.0 (psi).

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay, cabin pressure's coming up. (Correcting himself) Suit pressure's coming up - in the cabin.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: We might as well turn the urine-line heater off. [While performing the tasks on Surface 2-1, they emptied the urine collection bags in their suits into a transfer line which led, ultimately, to a collection tank in the descent stage. The heater prevents the line from freezing.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Yeah. Right. For now. (Long Pause) Okay, mine's off of the peg on the cuff gauge. [The cuff-mounted pressure gauges do not go down to zero.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1063500csm.text: Endeavour, Houston. You're T-2 now.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1063500csm.text: Roger. I have the landing site in view.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1063500csm.text: Roger. Very good.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: (Garbled) on mine (Pause) Want to take it up to 3.7?

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Yeah. (Pause)

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay, there's 3.5.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Right.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: 3.6, 3.65. Okay. I'm (setting Reg B to) Egress (thereby cutting off the oxygen flow). Reading 3.6.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay. One minute. [They will now monitor the suits for one minute.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay. You hack (that is, note) the time?

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Yeah. (Long Pause)

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay. And, Houston; Endeavour. I've got the LM.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1063500csm.text: Roger, Al.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1063500csm.text: I'll give you the coordinates in a minute.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1063500csm.text: But he's almost directly north of Index.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1063500csm.text: Roger. Understand. [Long pause.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1063500csm.text: Dave and Jim, while you're timing that minute out, be advised that Endeavour is passing overhead. Al's got you in sight, and I suspect there are two big cameras (the pan camera and the mapping camera, both in the SIM Bay) that'll be brought to bear on you a little later on.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay, very good. I'll bet Al can tell you where we are better than we can.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1063500csm.text: Al says you're...

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay, Joe; that's a minute, and...

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1063500csm.text: ...just north of Index.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: ...I've got...(Pause)

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: North of Index, huh? [The following is the conversation between Al Worden and Gordon Fullerton regarding Worden's observations of the landing site through the Command Module Sextant.] 106:38:10 Worden: I have the landing site in view. 106:38:13 Fullerton: Roger. Very Good. 106:38:29 Worden: Okay. And, Houston, Endeavour. I've got the LM. 106:39:34 Fullerton: Roger, Al. 106:39:39 Worden: I'll give you the coordinates in a minute. 106:39:41 Fullerton: Okay. 106:39:43 Worden: But he's almost directly north of Index. 106:39:46 Fullerton: Roger. Understand. 106:40:28 Fullerton: Endeavour, Houston.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1063500csm.text: Endeavour, Houston. You're TCA now.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay, I'm reading 3.4. [Jim's suit pressure has reduced by 0.2 psi due to breathe-down, minor leaks, and flow into nooks and crannies. Anything less than a 0.3 psi decrease in one minute is acceptable.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay. Okay. I'm reading 3.4. That's 2/10ths in a minute. (Pause) Okay, Suit Circuit Relief (Valve) to Auto.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1063500csm.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1063500csm.text: Circuit Relief going Auto. (Pause) [With the pressure integrity check complete, they have now reset the relief valve so that it will open if the pressure in the Suit Circuit exceeds 5.3 psi.]

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1063500csm.text: Okay. He's about half way between Index and the next crater off towards the North Complex. He's sitting right by a very small crater. And, as soon as I lose them here, I'll give you the coordinates, but he's quite plain down there.

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1063500csm.text: Suit circuit pressure should go down to 4.8. (Long Pause) [They are now on Surface 2-3.] Post-landing Activities Apollo 15 Journal Stand-up EVA

a15_1063500csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1063500csm.text: Roger, Al.

a15a1064115.speaker: Allen
a15a1064115.text: And, Falcon, you are Go for depress.

a15a1064115.speaker: Scott
a15a1064115.text: Roger; understand Go for depress. [Readers should note that, according to the Apollo 15 Final Lunar Surface Procedures document, Dave and Jim had planned to start the SEVA at about 106:10. Consequently, they are about 30 minutes behind the nominal timeline.]

a15a1064115.speaker: Scott
a15a1064115.text: Okay, we're down almost to 5 on the gauge.

a15a1064115.speaker: Irwin
a15a1064115.text: Cabin Repress coming open. (Pause) Open! [By opening this circuit breaker on the panel ( CB(16) ) at Jim's right shoulder, they are preventing any possibility that the ECS will try to repressurize the cabin once they open the dump valve .]

a15a1064115.speaker: Scott
a15a1064115.text: Okay, overhead or forward dump valve Open, then Auto, at three and a half (psi). (Pause) [Jim will open the dump valve in the hatch until the cabin pressure drops to 3.5 psi. At that point, he will close it by going to the Auto position so that they can monitor the response of the Suit Circuit to the reduced cabin pressure.]

a15a1064115.speaker: Scott
a15a1064115.text: Verify cabin pressure 3.5, LM suit circuit lockup at 4.3. Okay, the LM suit circuit about 4.5 (psi). (Pause) And it's (pause) stable. (Pause)

a15a1064115.speaker: Worden
a15a1064115.text: Okay, Gordo. If you look at the grid map, 1 to 250; that's HR25-11, he's on BR, .5, 75.5.

a15a1064115.speaker: Irwin
a15a1064115.text: Yeah, it looks like it's locked up.

a15a1064115.speaker: Scott
a15a1064115.text: Okay, overhead...I mean, forward dump valve to Open and verify LM suit circuit 3 (garbled, but undoubtedly '3.6 to 4.3').

a15a1064115.text: Ready to turn the card? [Rather than using the Surface Checklist Book, they are using a large cue card which they have mounted on the panel in front of them.] [Scott - "The Cue Cards were a major and formal part of the procedures and of the checklist system."]

a15a1064115.speaker: Irwin
a15a1064115.text: I'll hold it if you'll push it on there.

a15a1064115.text: Okay, hatch opening. [This is the overhead, docking hatch normally used in orbit for transfers between the LM and the Command Module.]

a15a1064115.speaker: Scott
a15a1064115.text: Well, I guess. (Garbled) Okay, it's partially open.

a15a1064115.speaker: Irwin
a15a1064115.text: Okay, I'm going to go Auto on the dump valve here.

a15a1064115.speaker: Irwin
a15a1064115.text: Okay, I'm Auto on the forward dump valve.

a15a1064115.speaker: Irwin
a15a1064115.text: Okay. "Overhead hatch: full open and latched."

a15a1064115.speaker: Scott
a15a1064115.text: Okay, coming full open. (Pause) [Jones - "Did the hatch swing down into the cabin and, if so, was it hinged at the back?"] [Scott - "Yeah, and there's a latch at the back (of the cabin) that locks it in, as I recall. This was a very easy procedure, relatively speaking, and it's interesting, when we got into it, how straight-forward it was - almost to the extent that the LM almost might have been designed to do this."] [Jones - "I'll have to ask why the 16 and 17 crews didn't do it."] [Scott - "I don't know, but it was easy to do and I thought we got a lot of benefit out of it."]

a15a1064115.speaker: Allen
a15a1064115.text: Roger. Endeavour places you very near November Crater; very close to November Crater.

a15a1064115.speaker: Scott
a15a1064115.text: Okay. A little short (that is, east), huh? (Pause)

a15a1064115.speaker: Allen
a15a1064115.text: A little short and a little north. [A detail from Pan camera frame 9377, which will be taken in about one hour, shows the LM on the northwest rim of Last Crater. November is the sharp-rimmed crater farther east. The planned landing spot is just off the bottom of the image, about 200 meters south of the southern rim of Last. Stephen Tellier has provided a higher-resolution detail of the area immediately around the LM.]

a15a1064115.speaker: Irwin
a15a1064115.text: Okay, Dave, you got the hatch open?

a15a1064115.speaker: Scott
a15a1064115.text: Okay. (Garbled). Forgot about the LCG (garbled) ISA. (Long Pause) [The Interim Stowage Assembly ( ISA ) is a set of cloth bags on a frame that fits over Dave's wall-mounted PLSS immediately behind his flight station. An ISA can be seen on the left at Neil Armstrong's back in Apollo 11 training photo KSC-69PC-319 . The dialog suggests that Dave has caught his LM hoses on the ISA. Water is circulated through these tubes and carries away exces

a15a1064115.speaker: Irwin
a15a1064115.text: Push them (possibly Dave's hoses) out of the way? [After opening the hatch, Dave will sit on the engine cover and reach up to remove the docking drogue. Once he removes the drogue, he will hand it to Jim who, in turn, will put it on the floor on the left side of the cabin. Here, Dave may be getting himself into position on the engine cover. His hoses come across the cabin from the ECS which is behind Jim's station.]

a15a1064115.speaker: Scott
a15a1064115.text: Yeah. All right, give me a little...

a15a1064115.speaker: Irwin
a15a1064115.text: What do you want me to do?

a15a1064115.speaker: Irwin
a15a1064115.text: Okay. (Pause) Okay, are you sitting up there now?

a15a1064115.text: Yeah, just stand by. (Long Pause) Okay. (Pause) Okay, overhead hatch is open and latched.

a15a1064115.speaker: Irwin
a15a1064115.text: Okay. (Reading) Sit on the engine cover, facing forward, unlock the drogue, and rotate counter-clockwise to release.

a15a1064115.speaker: Irwin
a15a1064115.text: (As per checklist) I'll block the sun from impinging on the instrument panel.

a15a1064115.speaker: Irwin
a15a1064115.text: (I'm a) shadow device. (Long Pause) [Jones - "Why was it necessary to shade the instrument panel?"] [Scott - "So it won't get too hot. It wasn't really designed to take the heat."]

a15a1064115.speaker: Irwin
a15a1064115.text: I just (garbled). [Dave is probably handing the drogue to Jim.]

a15a1064115.speaker: Scott
a15a1064115.text: Why don't you...Wait, wait. (Watch out for the) utility lights. That a boy. Okay, you got it?

a15a1064115.speaker: Irwin
a15a1064115.text: I've got it. (Long Pause) [Scott, from the 1971 Technical Debrief - "(Getting the drogue out) was very similar to the one-sixth-g airplane exercises we had."]

a15a1064115.speaker: Irwin
a15a1064115.text: Okay. 106:48:01 Scott: Give me the next step (in the procedure). (Pause) Go ahead, Jim; read the next step.

a15_1064802csm.speaker: Fullerton

a15_1064802csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1064802csm.text: (Garbled) (Pause) Turn up the...The Annun-Num lights there. [The brightness of the Annunciator/Numerics lights on the control panels can be adjusted.]

a15_1064802csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1064802csm.text: Oh boy, what a view. a15_1065022csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1065022csm.text: Houston, Endeavour. The - the Gamma-ray boom is out and took 2:30; 2 minutes and 30 seconds, fixed in.

a15_1065022csm.text: Beautiful!

a15_1065022csm.text: Fantastic.

a15_1065022csm.speaker: Scott

a15_1065022csm.text: Okay.

a15_1065022csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1065022csm.text: Endeavour, Houston. One other thing, if you don't have it already, we'd like to have the S-Band Squelch, Off, so you'll realize the loss of signal, Over.

a15_1065022csm.text: Rog, Gordo. I've got it Off now.

a15_1065022csm.text: Roger.

[Note that Joe makes this transmission on his own initiative, conscious that the Flight Director wants to keep close to the timeline.] [In principle, these bearings can be used to triangulate an accurate LM location. a15_1065022csm.text: Roger. (Pause) [In Houston, the Flight Director tells Joe that Dave should get one or two more bearings. "It won't take long to get 'em."]

a15_1065022csm.text: Okay.

a15_1065022csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1065022csm.text: No, I can't right now, Joe.

a15_1065022csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1065022csm.text: Roger.

a15_1065022csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1065022csm.text: I'll get on with the photography here. 106:53:45 Allen: Roger; we agree. (Pause)

a15_1065022csm.text: Right. a15_1065022csm.text: Roger. (Pause) We'll worry about those when we start driving in Pluton. [Frame AS15-85- 11359 shows these boulders. They are about 3500 meters from the spacecraft.]

a15_1065022csm.text: Dave, can you see the edge of the rille?

a15_1065022csm.text: Nope. (Pause) [Jim is asking about the closest portion of the rille, due west of them. Photo AS15-85= 11356 shows a bend in the rille in the direction of Hill 305 .]

a15_1065022csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1065022csm.text: And, Dave, while you're swinging (turning) around there, do you know if you can see November (Crater) yet or not?

a15_1065022csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1065022csm.text: I don't, Joe. I better try and get some photos here and then start thinking...

a15_1065022csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1065022csm.text: Roger.

a15_1065022csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1065022csm.text: ...about looking around. (Long Pause) I think, probably, we owe you the photos first.

a15_1065022csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1065022csm.text: Roger. We agree.

a15a1065723.speaker: Fullerton
a15a1065723.text: Endeavour, Houston. When you have a minute, I have another Pan Camera PAD.

a15a1065723.text: This one goes [in the box in the Flight Plan] at 108:10.

a15a1065723.text: Okay. T-start is 108:15:27, and T-stop is 108:43:15. Over.

But it's a way to explore the area, to go look at it. On field

a15a1065723.speaker: Scott
a15a1065723.text: Okay. And let me start by 12 o'clock (west), Joe, and I'll go around real quick. On the far distant horizon, apparently across the rille, I can see - just about our 1 o'clock, now - a very large mountain, which I'd have to call Hill 305 .

a15a1065723.speaker: Scott
a15a1065723.text: And all of the features around here are very smooth. The tops of the mountains are rounded off. There are no sharp jagged peaks or no large boulders apparent anywhere. The whole surface of the area appears to be smooth, with the largest fragments I can see are in the walls of Pluton. There are no boulders at all on St. George, Hill 305, Bennett (Hill) , or, as far as I can tell, looking back up at Hadley. Hadley's sort of in the shadow. It's a gently rolling terrain completely around 360 degrees; hummocky, much like you saw on 14. The ridge line across the rille, from Hill 305 around to 1 o'cl

a15_1070143csm.text: Okay, Houston; Endeavour. You've got the High Gain now.

a15_1070143csm.text: Okay. Coming on around to St. George, it again is a very subtle old crater, but in this case, I can see some lineaments dipping to the west at about 20 degrees, parallel to the rim of the crater. a15_1070143csm.text: And as far as ALSEP deployment...Ha! Unfortunately, looking straight ahead (that is, directly away from the Sun) in zero-phase, it's washed out somewhat, but if there's continuity of the surface that I see in our general position, I don't think we'll have any trouble taking the ALSEP out 300 (meters) or so and placing it. a15_1070809csm.text: Endeavour, Houston. Would you give us Auto on the High Gain.

a15_1070809csm.text: Roger, Houston. Auto on the High Gain.
