a15_1285501csm.text: Okay, that sounds good to us. Could you tell us whether the north-facing side of the Central Station can see any portion of the RTG (Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator)?

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1285501csm.text: No, it definitely cannot. Because the RTG is perhaps a little south of and east, as far as the Central Station's concerned.

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Parker
a15_1285501csm.text: And, Al, if you read, we'd like to have your DSE configured.

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Mission Control
a15_1285501csm.text: This is Apollo Control at 129 hours, 37 minutes. Our change of shift press briefing with the Gold Team is scheduled to begin shortly in the main auditorium of Building 1 at the Manned Spacecraft Center. We'll be reacquiring the Command Module in about 6 minutes. Al Worden is scheduled to begin a sleep period at about 133 hours, 20 minutes. The principal order of business with the Lunar Module crew, Jim Irwin and dave Scott, will be to get them to bed as soon as possible, and they have nearly completed the list of activities prior to beginning their rest period. During the change of shift brief

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1285501csm.text: Roger, we copy that. [Scott - "You could not take an RTG to the Moon, today. It would not be permitted. In fact, we were looking at power for the (unmanned, miniature) Rovers, on the Moon and Mars, and several of the documents I've seen said 'Consider anything but RTG's.' Gosh."]

a15_1285501csm.text: And, Dave, could you call out to us the problem with your yo-yo. And do you think it can be fixed?

a15_1285501csm.text: No, we looked at it when we got back in, Joe. The string broke at its attach point on the inside of the yo-yo (as shown in Figure 14-52 from the Mission Report ).

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1285501csm.text: Okay, Dave and Jim, you might want to consider switching out yo-yos. Jim, you may want to pass yours over to Dave for the next EVA.

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1285501csm.text: We've already done that, Joe.

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1285501csm.text: You're always one step ahead of me. [Jones - "Why would you need a functioning yo-yo? Because you were the tong wielder?"] [Scott - "I think so. But, why wouldn't Jim have tongs? It could be because I picked up the rock and Jim had the bag."] ["The tongs were excellent. They worked as advertised. They helped us overcome some of the need to bend over in the suit. In fact, the tongs grasped the rock better than you could with your hand. Good system."] [Jones - "Do the glove fingers need some work? I've always thought that was an area where the suits (need improvement)..."] [Scott - "Yeah, some p

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1285501csm.text: Some quick questions about the Rover, now. Could you confirm that battery 2 amp-voltmeter always reads zero, please.

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1285501csm.text: I guess I can't answer that, Joe. I could never see the amperage on 2 when we were driving.

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1285501csm.text: Okay, my answer, Joe, would be yes. I never saw a motion of that needle.

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1285501csm.text: Okay, that's plenty good enough for us. As you know, we think that you've got two good batteries, but possibly a failed meter there. And the Rover power consumption looks like it's right on the money, and we've got a lot of gas (battery charge) for the next EVAs. The amp-hour meter data which we have does have a couple of erratic points in it. We're wondering if you noticed any meter-movement anomalies. MP3 Audio Clip ( 12 min 05 sec ) by David Shaffer

a15a1290038.speaker: Irwin
a15a1290038.text: This is Jim. I didn't notice any meter motion or anomalies, Joe.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Okay, Jim, thank you. And we're assuming that the Rover is now parked facing north. Is that correct?

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: That's correct.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: I could have guessed as much. And a question about the suspension, which sounds kind of exciting. Did you ever notice it hitting bottom?

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Yes, we hit bottom a couple of times when we hit a rock, and it seemed to respond fairly well. I mean you could just feel that it had bottomed out. I might add something else, too, on your battery problem, Joe. I'm sure you're right about that because I noticed, in backing up a couple of times, that the front wheels did drive.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Okay, interesting comment, Dave. Thank you. Now we're getting on to the toughies here, and coming up to a very interesting one. We'd like to know what your best estimation of the LM's position is. Over.

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Stand by.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: And, Dave and Jim, let me give you some background on that. We've got several points that are in a very tight cluster around the first location we gave you. We think, however, because of bootstrapping a location from Elbow Crater backwards using the Rover navigation system, we think that you may be mistaking Last Crater for Index Crater. And I want you to consider this as you look at your map and think about your present position. Over.

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: My! [Comm Break] [Scott - "I remember all this discussion. In retrospect, it wasn't really significant - especially with the beauty of the Rover. You could be sort of anywhere in the area. If you're trying to make a pinpoint landing and walk to Surveyor, as Pete did, that's one thing. But if you're exploring a region with a Rover, you don't really care. And I think we all spent far too much time discussing where we were. In retrospect, we could have been forward or aft a kilometer and, for the purpose of what we did, there wouldn't be much effect. I mean, you wouldn't want to be too far east o

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Joe, you've stimulated an interesting discussion. Give us a couple of more minutes.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: We thought we might, Dave. (Pause) And, Dave and Jim, as you well know, this question is pretty much academic because we're doing great guns, no matter where your exact location is; and it's something we'll construct later (from the Rover Navigation readouts and the photography); but we're interested nonetheless. 129:05:07 Scott: Roger. (Long Pause) Okay, Joe. How about 73.3 Bravo Sierra 4? And I guess that's because we are on the northeast side of the double crater.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Voila! We understand.

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Sure nice that Rover will make 12, 13 clicks, isn't it?

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: That sure is. Richard (Gordon, the back-up commander)'s studying the maps here momentarily. In the meantime, could you give us just a rough guess - a quick rundown - as to where the samples at Station 1 were taken with respect to the rim of Elbow, and we're interested in distance and direction from the rim. Just a rough guess.

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Stand by. (Long Pause as he studies EVA-1/2, Part B) [Jones - "Let's see. Dick was the CMP on 12, right?"] [Scott - "Yeah. He was my backup on (Apollo) 15. And he was my backup on (Gemini) 8. We rotated."] 129:06:38 Scott: Okay, Joe, 70.9, Bravo Echo 5, and we moved out about 200 feet to the east of that point in picking up the three radial samples.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Okay, Dave, copied that loud and clear. And, by the way, Rover Nav system gave us exactly the same coordinates as you just called down for your LM location. Interesting coincidence, or perhaps not a coincidence.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Moving on to the next question. Near Elbow Crater, Dave, you mentioned that your footprints exposed white soil. We wonder if this was a common occurrence. Did you observe similar white soil in footprints elsewhere? Over.

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Joe, I sort of kicked through a rim of a small, l-meter, subdued crater; and, as I did that, I kicked up some white soil. And so I kicked a couple of more times and it spread out; and whether I was breaking up a very friable rock or not, I don't know. But there was a couple of kickfuls of dirt that were white, and as we came back past it on the return trip to the LM, why, I pointed it out to Jim and he saw it too. And I'm not sure whether that was just at that one small crater, which was an old crater, or whether that was typical of that particular area. We just didn't have time to look at it.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Roger, Dave. Copy that. And coming back to Station 1, Elbow Crater, could you give us a quick rundown on the changes in block distribution around Elbow Crater and, if possible, maybe even the changes in rock types there. Over.

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Stand by one. (Long Pause) Joe, our clocks were running pretty fast when we were there, and I guess we didn't get a chance to look at the distribution very well. As I remember it, there were more blocks - not really blocks, but large fragments on the order of 6 inches to a foot (in size) - more on the southern rim, although it wasn't really heavily concentrated; I'd say 10 percent of the surface at most (was covered with pieces of rock). There was more on the southern rim than on the northern rim. And the ones we sampled all looked pretty much the same. As I remember, the radial sample didn't

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Roger, Dave. We copy that, and answers that question very well. But, once again, regarding Elbow Crater; Jim, you called out to us a bench around the east side of Elbow and you were looking down into Elbow from higher up on the front. We wonder if you could compare that bench with breaks in the slope of the Rille wall. Over. (Long Pause) [That is, is there any evidence that both Elbow Crater and the rille wall are showing signs of near-surface structure in the underlying layers of bedrock.]

a15a1290038.speaker: Irwin
a15a1290038.text: Joe, when I commented on "bench", I would estimate there are two or three different levels that were very-subdued, possible benches in Elbow. And I did not see any immediate relation between those subdued benches in Elbow and the Rille.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Okay, Jim, copy that. That sounds very reasonable. We'd like to move on down towards Station 2 now, and have a series of questions about Station 2. The first one being, what rock samples did you get from Station 2, and we're more interested in the samples that did not come from the large boulder, but rather what other samples did you get there? Over.

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Okay, stand by. (Long Pause) Okay, Joe, our sum total at Station 2 was two chips off the large rock, soil from the fillet, soil adjacent about a couple of feet away from the rock, soil from beneath the rock, and the double core, and the comprehensive.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Okay, Dave, you called it right on from memory. That's exactly the score sheet we had. (Pause) Stand by a second. Let me read over this second question. Okay...

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Okay, Joe. ...

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: ...regarding the boulder, do you think, possibly, that the black part of the boulder might be a big clast in a coarse breccia? Over.

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: No, I'm not sure, Joe. The breccia that was in there was glass covered, and there was an exposure after I took a chip out of it that was a breccia not unlike 14's (that is, the Apollo 14 samples). As a matter of fact, I'd say it was almost typical of 14's, but maybe only second or third order. [A first-order breccia is a rock composed of fragments which, individually, are composed of a single rock type. A second-order breccia consists of fragments which, individually, are breccias. That is, fragments made of smaller fragments. And so on.]

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: There definitely was a linear...I called it a contact. Whether it might have been a very large clast inside a very large rock, there's no telling. But there was a definite line there which differentiated two types of rock within that big boulder, and I really wouldn't want to guess whether that was a large clast or not.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Okay, Dave, sounds good. Could you tell us where the samples which came off the boulder were taken in relation to this contact that you called out on the boulder? In other words, where did the chips come loose from? Over. MP3 Audio Clip ( 12 min 32 sec ) by David Shaffer

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Okay; if you consider the boulder being divided in fifths, 1/5th of it was a different type, apparently, by this sort of topographic contact. We took one chip from that side and one chip from a corner on the other side.

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: We copy that; thank you. We'd like for you to summarize the relationships of mare and Apennine Front in the Elbow-St. George area. And, we're looking for any evidence whatever of a contact, an albedo change, or a change in coarse-frag abundance. Over.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Joe, we looked, and we discussed it before we went out, and we've discussed it since we came back, and we honestly didn't see anything.

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Roger, Dave; and you discussed it, then, about the same way during the traverse. So it sounds very consistent to us. Do you think that you can drive to either Spur or to Window Crater (which are planned EVA-2 stops on the flank of Mt. Hadley Delta).

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Let us take a look here, quick. (Long Pause) Well, there are a number of craters down there in the area of Spur and Window, and those are the only craters up on the Apennine Front. And there are several the same size as Spur and Window, which I think were not evident on the photography because of the (relatively high) albedo and the Sun. I think we could get to some of those craters, yes. I'm not sure it would be Spur or Window, but there are some craters up on the side of the Front I'm fairly sure we could get to.

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Roger, Dave. Copy that. And that is exactly the answer we were after; not necessarily those particular craters, but craters similar to them; and we understand exactly what you're saying. [The geologic interest is in finding one or more relatively fresh craters which have penetrated through the soil layer and exposed fragments of rocks of which the mountain is made.]

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: We'd like to ask: "Was the abundance of white and light-gray rocks described in the vicinity of Falcon the same seen along the entire route to St. George, or did this abundance of white and light-gray rocks seem to vary?" Over.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Joe, I think we have a great variety of fragments out here. I...I wouldn't want to pin down any particular type in any area until we had more time to look. We've got a couple of surprises for you. We have one fragment (the Seatbelt Basalt) on the order of 6 inches which is a fairly well rounded, highly vesicular basalt with vesicles on the order of 3 millimeters all over it, apparently quite old and rounded, and it's a brownish gray. We also have a large piece of glass, just sheer glass, apparently, which is about a foot long and about 6 inches wide and very rough-textured surface; and that wa

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Roger, Dave. Read you loud and clear on that, and that really brings us to our last question. We're in the process of starting to plan your traverse tomorrow. It's going to be a good one. We have no equipment problems that we're looking at right now and we'd like to ask you if there're any particular inputs you would like to make into the planning team regarding tomorrow's traverse. Over.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Okay, let us talk it over a minute, please. [Comm Break] [Scott - "Silver used to debrief us on field trips . It's too bad we didn't take this transcript and the photos, and sit down and spend a year going back through it. I wonder if that would have been scientifically useful. It would have been interesting, but would it have contributed much more to what they learned anyway?"] [Jones - "We've talked about it in the context of the Mars mission - that part of the job of the crew is to spend the voyage back going through the material and doing thorough debriefs."] [Scott - "Absolutely. Nine mon

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Joe, we've talked it over, and we think the best thing to do is to stick exactly with the plan we have now. I think we understand what we're looking for, and even though we didn't find some of the things we were looking for today (crystalline rocks, in particular), that doesn't mean that we won't find them as we head down to Front Crater. And I guess about the only input we'd have would be that, if we can make as good a time on the Rover tomorrow as we did today, perhaps we'd have more time to sample a variety of stations along the Front and on the way back. But, in general, I think we'd do be

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Right on, Dave. We copy that, and I think we're going that direction. Sounds good. We got a couple more general questions and then a comment about the 16-millimeter camera, and after that we're going to be closing up shop down here. One more geology question. Do you have any feel for whether the frags around the small fresh craters that you've called out to us are, in general, pieces of the projectile or do you think they're ejecta frags? Over.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Well, Joe, we're pretty sure they're projectile frags, and that's one (type of crater) we really need to stop and sample. 129:22:12 Allen: Agreed, Dave. We think the same thing here. A quick comment on your 16-millimeter film. We think that that camera, the DAC, is still in good shape. That Mag Charlie was a bad magazine, and we think you can help us out on the other magazines left, tomorrow, by advancing the film with your finger just to make sure it's moving freely in the magazine before you clip it onto the camera itself.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: That's a grand analysis, Joe. We're ...

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: And that's something you can do while you're packing the ETB. Can do it tonight. Over.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Rog, Joe. That's a good analysis. We took Mag Charlie and tried to run it with our fingers and it won't run. It's absolutely jammed right in the beginning. And we'll run the others through tonight to make sure they'll work. [See the discussion following 120:36:40 .]

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Sounds terrific. And, Dave and Jim, we'll be standing by for a crew status report. No hurry on that; and, as I say, we're going to close up shop down here. We've got more data, really, than we know what to do with. But we'll work hard on it and be back with you in the morning. I do have (a) lift-off time Pad to send to you, Jim, when you're ready to copy.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Okay, he's got his pencil out. Go ahead. [Jones - "There were, in fact, forms with blank spaces? And did you mean a literal 'pencil'."] [Scott - "And pens. I've still got my pencils. Most of the time I think we used Pentels, which were the first felt-tipped pens. In fact, we used those back on Gemini."] [Jones - "Capillary feed rather than gravity feed."] [Scott - "Every time that we need to write down something that the ground reads up to us, there is a block in the flight plan to record that data, or in the checklist or whatever is appropriate at that time. You don't just get a blank piece o

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Readback's correct. Jim, you've been doing good work all day.

a15a1291348.speaker: Irwin
a15a1291348.text: Well, we're trying. (Pause)

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Roger. And, Dave and Jim, one last comment, which we're pretty sure you're aware of. We think we're looking at an EVA tomorrow that'll run about six and a half hours, about the same thing we did today. And we do have a few miscellaneous (ALSEP) items to clean up, most likely at the end of the traverse, so it's liable to be a little shorter distancewise, but otherwise, other than that, it'll be more or less unchanged. Over.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Okay, very good, Joe. By the way, did you notice that I had a higher O2 usage all the way through, and is that why we're looking at six and a half instead of seven hours?

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: That's correct, Dave. We've got very good data points on you. It's a steady curve, and the O2 rate is just a little bit higher than we predicted. From the looks of it, you've really been doing some work up there.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Well, do you have any idea why there's a rate? Perhaps maybe a (suit) zipper could be lubricated or something like that?

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Dave, this is a metabolic curve, plain and simple. It's not a leak rate at all. [Jones - "What does Joe mean by 'metabolic rate'? That, when you were working harder, the use rate went up more than expected?"] [Scott - "Yeah, I discussed that when I was down in Houston (being interviewed about the suits). Let me recall if I can...I don't know how they plan the metabolic rate but, obviously, the amount of "work" work that you do determines the amount of oxygen you consume. So they were looking at the consumption of the oxygen, I guess, relative to the heart rate and everything else. And that giv

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Okay, well, I'll breathe a little less tomorrow.

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: We don't recommend that - (joking) although the Surgeon's working on it right now. The numbers though, actually that we're coming up with, Dave, is about...The two numbers are 1150 Btu's per hour, working; and about 700 Btu's, riding. Over.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Okay; that's a little higher on the riding than I think we expected, but it's sort of a sporty job to drive this thing to make sure we don't run into the craters; and if you can get that front steering figured out, it'll sure help. (Pause)

a15a1291348.speaker: Slayton
a15a1291348.text: Get six and a half hours like you did today, guys. Nobody's going to complain.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Okay. Roger. (Long Pause) [Scott - "There is an excellent book written by a guy named Baker in England. It's almost a coffee-table book. But it's almost all words. He put it out in the mid-70's. It weighs a ton. But it is really good. He has gone through Mercury, Gemini, Apollo. All the flights. And, in the back he has tables of the quantitative information related to each flight. Just an excellent source."] [Journal Contributor David Harland notes that the book is "The History of Manned Spaceflight" by David Baker and published in 1981 by New Cavendish Books, London. Harland agrees that " it

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Dave and Jim, I'm going to sign off now, and I'm getting excited about tomorrow's traverse already. And Bob (Parker)'s coming on. Over.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Okay, Joe. You did a superfine job today, and we sure appreciate you keeping track of us and keep us going in a straight line. We'll be looking forward to seeing you tomorrow.

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Yes, sir, wouldn't miss it for the world. [Long Comm Break] MP3 Audio Clip ( 12 min 18 sec ) by David Shaffer

a15a1293238.speaker: Parker
a15a1293238.text: And, Falcon, we'd like biomed, right, please. [Houston wants to look at telemetry from Jim's sensors. Biomed left would give them Dave's telemetry.]

a15a1293238.speaker: Scott
a15a1293238.text: Okay, biomed right. There's nothing there right now (that is, Jim does not have his sensors on), but we'll give it to you.

a15a1293238.speaker: Parker
a15a1293238.text: Roger. Yes. We understand. [Very Long Comm Break. During this half hour, Dave and Jim are probably finishing their meal.]

Looks very distinctly like the roof, or the - the top of the rille is collapsed in some places, and the rille is exposed in other places.

But it looks very much like portions of - the - the rille have a collapsed roof. And, in fact, the one I was looking at, works it's way into what looks like one of the - one of the ridges. It was very ridgy to the - to the north and then turned into a rille as it went south.

a15_1414815csm.text: Okay, you're still too loud. You got a squeal.

a15_1414815csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1414815csm.text: Yeah, I'll turn it down a little bit. How's that?

a15_1414815csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1414815csm.text: That's better. Okay. (Reading) " CB(11) Comm, CDR Audio, open, and connected to PLSS comm ." In work. (Long Pause) Okay, I'm in B, I have a Press flag and an O; O2 Momentary. Pressure gauge, and how do you read, Jim?

a15_1414815csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1414815csm.text: I read you loud and clear.

a15_1414815csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1414815csm.text: Okay, you have to check with Houston.

a15_1414815csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1414815csm.text: Dave and Jim, we read you both loud and clear. MP3 Audio Clip ( 19 min 30 sec ) by David Shaffer

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Okay, they read me loud and clear.

a15a1415133.speaker: Allen
a15a1415133.text: Roger. Go on to next step.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: PLSS mode for you to B and me to A. (Pause)

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay, how do you read, Jim?

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Loud and clear.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay, you're loud and clear to me, and Houston, how do you read the CDR?

a15a1415133.speaker: Allen
a15a1415133.text: Roger. You're both 5 by.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay. Let's both go to AR.

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: AR.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay, AR. You're loud and clear to me; how me to you?

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Same.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay, Houston. How do you read the LMP and the CDR again? And how's your TM?

a15a1415133.speaker: Allen
a15a1415133.text: Okay, Dave. We're loud and clear on both, and we're Go for the next step.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay. My PLSS O2 quantity is 90 percent. How about yours, Jim?

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Reading 92.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay. "CB(16) ECS, LCG Pump, close."

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Closed.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay. "LCG, cold as required." [Once they turn off the LM LCG pump, they won't have cooling until they have depressurized the cabin and have started PLSS cooling. Here, they are taking one last opportunity to cool down before shutting off the pump and disconnecting the LM water hoses. Pete Conrad and Al Bean added this cool-down step, on their own, during the preparations for their first Apollo 12 EVA. See the Apollo 12 Lunar Surface Journal at 114:53:38 and following.] [Scott - "An example of procedures evolution."]

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: "CB(16) ECS Cabin Repress, close; verify."

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Verified.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: "Suit Fan Delta-P, open."

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Open.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: "Suit Fan 2, open."

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Open.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay. "Verify ECS caution and H2O SEP component lights on, about a minute." (Pause) And there they come. (Pause) Oop, got a tone. Yeah; okay. (Pause) [They are now on checklist page 6-5.]

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: " Suit Gas Diverter (Valve) , Pull-Egress; verify."

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: That's verified.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: " Cabin Gas Return (Valve) , Egress; verify."

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: That's verified.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: " Suit Circuit Relief (Valve), Auto; verify."

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: That's verified.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay. "OPS connect; LMP first. Suit Isolation (Valve) to Suit Disconnect."

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Suit Disconnect.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay. Why don't you slip around here? (Pause) (I'll) get your OPS. (Pause) That water is cold, isn't it? (Pause) Okay. "OPS O2 hose to PGA blue to blue." (Long Pause)

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: I'll turn off the LCG Pump. (Dave laughs, probably because he is getting quite cold) (Pause) [Scott - "When my water started going through...I mean, it was a great system. Your whole body, all of a sudden, got cool!"]

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay. That's closed and locked. What's the next\ step? (Garbled) Look where I'm hooked again. I'm hooked the same place. The PLSS stowage handle.

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Okay. "Retrieve purge valve, verify closed; and lock pin, In and Lo. Install purge valve red to red."

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay. (Yawns; Long Pause) Okay. Purge valve is in, and locked, and locked.

a15a1415133.speaker: Worden
a15a1415133.text: Roger, Karl. We can check that out, and - if we don't see anything there, we can check it out during the EVA.

a15a1415133.speaker: Henize
a15a1415133.text: Very good. Good idea. On the...

a15a1415133.speaker: Worden
a15a1415133.text: And, the Mass Spectrometer is now fully retracted. Talkback is gray.

a15a1415133.speaker: Henize
a15a1415133.text: Wonderful. Just recycling it a couple of times, and it finally came in; is that what happened?

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Okay, (PGA) diverter valve's going vertical. (Pause) Okay, repeat on you. [As shown in Figure I-23 in the EMU Handbook , the diverter valve is part of the oxygen inflow connector and gives them the option of directing the PLSS oxygen flow entirely into the helmet (the vertical position) or partly into the suit torso (the horizontal position). Generally, the astronauts put the diverter valve to horizontal only when they were in the cabin and were trying to dry the suits out a little. In the hoizontal position, used in the cabin, all the incoming oxygen stream is divided between a duct leading t

a15a1415133.speaker: Worden
a15a1415133.text: Well, it took - I guess probably a half a dozen re - just recycles, jogging it out, then pulling it back in again and that may be - that may be the problem. Maybe that cable is kinking some way or other.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay. You're going to have to...Yeah, suit disconnect.

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Suit disconnect...

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Get...My O2 hose has just sort of drifted up there.

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Okay. (Pause) Okay.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay.

a15a1415133.speaker: Henize
a15a1415133.text: Okay. Real glad to hear you got that gray talkback.

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Okay, I'll disconnect your (LM O2) hoses. (Pause) And we'll connect the PLSS O2 hose. (Pause) In (and) locked.

a15a1415133.speaker: Henize
a15a1415133.text: Incidentally, the boys on the surface just about took a shower bath this morning. They had a small water leak in the gun there that let loose a couple of gallons of water. It was a major perturbation, although they've got it cleaned up pretty well. And they're running about an hour, to an hour and a half behind their time line on the second EVA. They haven't got out yet.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay.

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Okay. The purge valve. (Pause) Very low. (Pause) Okay, all locked, and the pin's in. (Long Pause) Okay. And it's locked.

a15a1415133.speaker: Worden
a15a1415133.text: Roger. Understand. [Pause.]

a15a1415133.speaker: Henize
a15a1415133.text: Okay, Al. We have about 10 seconds before we give an Image Motion Increase for the Mapping Camera.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay. "PGA diverter valve to vertical." Take a little drink. (Pause) Did you turn the Descent Water off? (Pause)

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Hose (garbled) last... (Pause)

a15a1415133.speaker: Allen
a15a1415133.text: Dave, that Descent Water was turned off on your PLSS recharge exercise.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Rog. We figured that out. It's working okay.

a15a1415133.speaker: Allen
a15a1415133.text: Roger.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay.

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Descent water closed. And stow that hose properly.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Yeah, man.

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Put it in the holster and I'll...

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay.

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: ...(get the) cable stowed (Long Pause)

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay; it's stowed. (Pause) Okay, helmet and gloves donning. (Pause) Okay. "Position mikes, both. PLSS fans on, Right. Vent flag clear." (Pause) Okay, my fan's coming on. Got a tone. Vent flag's clear. (Pause) (Looking at Jim's RCU ) Okay, your vent flag's clear. Let's get your LEVA . (Pause)

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: That's yours.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Yeah. (Pause)

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Put the flaps...

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Yeah. (Pause) Okay; let me get your water (that is, the in-suit drink bag ). And your food stick . (Pause)

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Here, I'll line it up.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Yeah, you line it up and I'll push it.

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: Okay, it's lined up.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: Okay. Wait, let me get this...(Long Pause)

a15a1415133.speaker: Irwin
a15a1415133.text: That did it.

a15a1415133.speaker: Scott
a15a1415133.text: (Chuckles) (Pause) There. Closed and locked. Let's get the back flap. (Long Pause) Okay; front flap. My turn. (Pause) [Next, they will get Dave's helmet on.]

a15_1420059csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1420059csm.text: Endeavour, this is Houston. You have 30 seconds until Pan Camera Mode goes to Standby.

a15_1420059csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420059csm.text: Okay, you watch my water spigot there?

a15_1420059csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420059csm.text: You may have to push it some.

a15_1420059csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1420059csm.text: No. (Brief Pause) You'll have to rotate the helmet, too. Shift it just a little bit. (Pause) No; too much. Shift it back. A little bit more. A little more to the right. A little more. A little more. That's good. Back a little to the left. That's right on.

a15_1420059csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420059csm.text: Okay. (Long Pause) Okay; secure the self-doffing straps. (Pause) Helmets. (Pause) (Garbled) (Pause)

a15_1420059csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420059csm.text: Okay. (Pause) Okay, LCG is cold. Yeah.

a15_1420059csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420059csm.text: Get back to your little corner.

a15_1420059csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1420059csm.text: LCG pump (circuit breaker) coming open. It's open now.

a15_1420059csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420059csm.text: Okay. "Disconnect LM water hoses and connect the PLSS water hoses."

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1420323csm.text: Al, we're still waiting for a cue on the lens stow, and in the meantime, photo target 25 is roaring down on us.

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1420323csm.text: Rog, got it in sight. [Long pause.]

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1420323csm.text: Push them just as far back as you possibly can, Dave.

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420323csm.text: Yeah, I will. (Long Pause) Yeah, they're snapped in the ECS handhold. I think they'll hold today. (Pause) Okay. You got your hoses stowed?

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1420323csm.text: Endeavour, Houston. We can go Pan Camera Power, Off.

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420323csm.text: Okay. Do a 180 here, and we'll check all the connectors.

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1420323csm.text: Okay. "Helmet and visor aligned and adjusted."

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420323csm.text: Okay. Let me put the booties (that is, the connector dust covers) on here. (Pause) The purge valve is locked.

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420323csm.text: Okay. "Helmet and visor, aligned and adjusted."

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420323csm.text: Okay. Let's take another look at the circuit breaker configuration.

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420323csm.text: "White Dots out plus EVA decals." (Long Pause) [They are checking to make sure that the circuit breakers and switches conform to the chart on Surface Checklist page 1-7. Circuit breakers marked as white in the diagram should be open (pulled out) while marked as black should be closed (pushed in).]

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420323csm.text: And mine are configured. [Next, they will start the glove-donning procedures on checklist page 6-6.]

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420323csm.text: That old graphite makes the hands slide in pretty easy, doesn't it?

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1420323csm.text: (Laughing) It doesn't do too good on the wrist connector though, does it? It makes it a little bit...(Pause)

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420323csm.text: Okay, I got two (gloves) on and locked. Come over and check mine when you get through. (Pause)

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420323csm.text: Okay. Gimme a call if you want a hand.

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420323csm.text: Okay. (Garbled) there. (Checking Jim's glove) Okay; got a lock and a lock. Okay. (Pause) Okay. Cuff's up. Okay. "PGA Diverter to Min; verify."

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420323csm.text: Okay, and "PLSS Pump, On, to the right."

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420323csm.text: Okay, " Press Reg A and B to Egress."

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1420323csm.text: A and B going to Egress.

a15_1420323csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420323csm.text: And we need a pressure integrity check. So next step is "PLSS O2 to On".

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1420949csm.text: Endeavour, this is Houston. When you get the camera stowed, I have one more small item, and then we'll give you some time to get out some food.

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1420949csm.text: Okay, my PLSS O2 is On.

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420949csm.text: And mine's On. (Pause) Okay, and the press flag should clear at 3.1 to 3.4 (psi). (Pause) I'm coming up. (Pause)

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1420949csm.text: Okay, Al - we're finding out that the - tight deadband in P20 is using a little more RCS propellant than we'd anticipated. Nothing's critical yet, but we would like to take - some preventive measures here. And we suggest that you go into the DAP - and load in a CSM weight of 30000, thirty thousand. And before you erase the current LM weight record it [corrects himself] the current CSM weight, record it for future use. We think that'll cut down the thruster firing a bit.

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1420949csm.text: Mine's clear. (Pause) [Apparently, Jim's O2 flag cleared almost immediately.]

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1420949csm.text: No, I'm sorry; no; I didn't clear the (tone)...

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420949csm.text: Yeah, there's your tone; yeah, mine too. (Long Pause) Okay, I'm off the peg.

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1420949csm.text: Okay, understand. Rog. You want me to go back and reload the DAP with a CSM weight of 30,000 and record the current weight that's in there for future use.

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420949csm.text: My flag's clear. (Pause) Okay, I'm stable at about 3.8. How about you?

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420949csm.text: Okay, if I can get that old O2 valve. Let's turn them off and do a little check.

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1420949csm.text: Okay, Falcon. We're marking a minute. [Joe means that Houston has started timing the one-minute pressure check.]

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420949csm.text: Okay, mine (meaning his PLSS O2)'s Off.

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420949csm.text: Okay. (Pause) And, Houston, we'll take your call when the minute's up.

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1420949csm.text: Roger. (Long Pause) Okay, Falcon. Mark 1 minute. Mickey's big hand went above his head. [This is a reference to the Mickey Mouse watches and clocks that many children grew up with in the 1940s and 50s.]

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420949csm.text: Okay. "Verify the O2 flag is clear." Mine is clear.

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420949csm.text: Okay, Houston. How do things look to you down there?

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1420949csm.text: Okay, Falcon; you're Go for depress.

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420949csm.text: Roger. Go for depress. Okay, Jim, "CB(16) ECS Cabin Repress, open."

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420949csm.text: Okay, overhead...I've got a little tone. (Pause) Okay, "forward dump valve , Open, and then, Auto, at 3.5." (Pause) Okay, keep my eyeball on the cabin pressure. I've got it. Okay; you can open it. (Pause)

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1420949csm.text: Open. [The sound of depressurization can be heard.]

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420949csm.text: "Verify cabin at 3.5." Okay, cabin's at 3.5. Suit circuit's locked up at about 4.4. My PGA is coming through 5 and decaying. And let's slip on a watch. [Dave may have had his watch hanging from the instrument panel and, in any event, he is now putting it on and is probably starting the stopwatch function.] [Scott, from a 1996 letter - "I do not recall ever having looked at my watch after egress. In the cabin after EVA-2, I noticed that the crystal of my Omega had popped off sometime during the EVA. Therefore, on EVA-3, I used my backup watch (which was) of a similar type. It worked just fine d

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420949csm.text: Okay. Ready. "Forward dump valve to Open." 142:14:44 Irwin: Okay, going Open. [The EVA has started.]

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420949csm.text: Okay. "Verify tone on and H2O flag at about 1.2 to 1.7." (Pause) Okay, 2.5; 2.0. Easy does it! (Pause) 1.5. (Long Pause) 0.5. (Pause) And what's your cuff gauge? (Pause)

a15_1420949csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1420949csm.text: Yeah, so am I. (Long Pause) And, we're about down to 0.2. Still reading about 5.1. (Pause) Are you at 5.1, also?

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1421615csm.text: Endeavour, a news bulletin from the surface says that they are now depressing the cabin; and there is no need for you to acknowledge. Keep eating.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1421615csm.text: Roger, Houston. Understand that, and - one point from here, Karl, - I'm over the spot in Imbrium, I think close to where you and Whitaker drew some, or figured out, some lava flows coming out of where the wrinkle ridge is, and at this low Sun angle, I can very clearly see some lava flows coming out of what appears to be a ridge, extending in both directions from the ridge. And I wasn't set up in time to take a picture of it, but it might be interesting on the next pass if we could get a - if we could get a PAD to take a picture of that.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1421615csm.text: Coming down [to] about 5.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1421615csm.text: Yeah.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1421615csm.text: We'll breath it down. (Pause)

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1421615csm.text: And, Falcon...

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1421615csm.text: Take a while at this rate.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1421615csm.text: ...the PLSSs look right on.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1421615csm.text: (Responding to Joe) Okay! Thank you.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1421615csm.text: Jim, your PLSS water recharge cured that problem we had yesterday completely, it looks like.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1421615csm.text: Good.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1421615csm.text: Yeah, it was worth the effort then. (Pause)

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1421615csm.text: Very interesting. Which window are you looking out?

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1421615csm.text: Those tones are a little disturbing. (Pause)

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1421615csm.text: I'm looking out window 3.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1421615csm.text: Window 3; that sounds like it's down to the south of you, then.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1421615csm.text: Just slightly north of groundtrack.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1421615csm.text: Okay. Well; " partially open the forward hatch." Maybe I can get that if you'll slip over there...

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1421615csm.text: Very good.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1421615csm.text: That's right. Just down in the south, just a little.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1421615csm.text: Thank you. Sounds like an interesting observation, and I'm sure the guys down below will be sending you up more work to do as a result. Be careful there, now.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1421615csm.text: A bit tight.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1421615csm.text: ...about as far as you can go. Careful not to get hooked. (Pause) That's it. Okay. (Long Pause) Okay, got a tone. (Long Pause)

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1421615csm.text: Can you reach around and hold the hatch so it doesn't blow shut? I got it. No sweat. It's a little easier today.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1421615csm.text: Getting in practice.

a15_1421615csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1421615csm.text: Yeah. a15a1421855.text: Let's see. Let me see if I can get around the hatch here and give you some more room.

a15a1421855.text: Well, maybe I can get my arm back there. (Pause) Yeah. I've got my arm back there. No sweat, Dave.

a15a1421855.speaker: Scott
a15a1421855.text: Oh, good.

a15a1421855.speaker: Irwin
a15a1421855.text: Find the control. (Pause)

a15a1421855.text: Okay. Mine's Open. (Long Pause) Get it okay?

a15a1421855.text: Just a minute. I think it's on. Yeah. It's on.

a15a1421855.speaker: Scott
a15a1421855.text: Okay. I'll tell you, my gloves feel a lot better today.

a15a1421855.text: (Laughs) Stretched them a little bit yesterday, Dave.

a15a1421855.text: Yeah. I think you're right. (Pause) Okay. "Rest until cooling sufficient", after we get the water going. And "verify the CWEA status". We might do that. The ECS and PREAMPS. Okay. (Pause) And I got a tone and a clear water flag. How about that? (Long Pause)

a15a1421855.text: Your water flag's clear, huh?

a15a1421855.speaker: Scott
a15a1421855.text: Yeah.

a15a1421855.text: Mine hasn't cleared yet. (Long Pause) 142:21:32 Scott: Okay. Let me get that (piece of duct) tape up by your left elbow.

a15a1421855.text: Okay, my water flag finally cleared.

a15a1421855.speaker: Scott
a15a1421855.text: Okay. (Pause) Okay, Houston. How does everything look to you down there? (Pause)

a15a1421855.text: Stand by, Dave.

a15a1421855.speaker: Scott
a15a1421855.text: Okay. (Pause)

a15a1422253.speaker: Scott
a15a1422253.text: Hey, Jim, let me get the old hatch open here. If you can...Okay...Yeah.

a15a1422253.speaker: Scott
a15a1422253.text: Okay. (Pause) Make it all right? (Pause)

a15a1422253.text: Okay, I'm around.

a15a1422253.speaker: Scott
a15a1422253.text: Okay.

a15a1422253.speaker: Irwin
a15a1422253.text: Get the hatch open a little farther today.

a15a1422253.speaker: Scott
a15a1422253.text: Oh, yeah; it's much better. (Pause) Okay, I'm going to come around this way today. (Pause) Little easier.

a15a1422253.speaker: Irwin
a15a1422253.text: Just me. [Dave may have bumped into Jim as he turned; and Jim is reassuring him that he hasn't hit any of the equipment.]

a15a1422253.speaker: Scott
a15a1422253.text: Okay. (Pause) Okay. (Pause)

a15a1422253.text: Whoa, Dave, whoa.

a15a1422253.text: Okay.

a15a1422253.speaker: Irwin
a15a1422253.text: Now you can get down. You were hung up on my RCU .

a15a1422253.speaker: Scott
a15a1422253.text: Okay. (Pause) How does that look to you? Okay?

a15a1422253.speaker: Irwin
a15a1422253.text: Yeah, that looks like you're pretty well cleared there. (Pause) You're well centered. I could get your (PLSS/OPS) antenna right now if you'd like.

a15a1422253.speaker: Scott
a15a1422253.text: No, let me get out.

a15a1422253.speaker: Irwin
a15a1422253.text: Okay. (Pause) Wanna hold right there?

a15a1422253.speaker: Scott
a15a1422253.text: Yeah. Why don't I hold here and you can get it.

a15a1422253.speaker: Irwin
a15a1422253.text: Okay. Your antenna is up. [Jim is on EVA-2 cuff checklist page LMP-3 and Dave is on CDR-3.]

a15a1422253.speaker: Scott
a15a1422253.text: Okay, you might check the...The water gun came out (of its stowage bracket) again.

a15a1422253.speaker: Irwin
a15a1422253.text: Sure did.

a15a1422253.speaker: Scott
a15a1422253.text: Okay. (Pause)

a15a1422253.speaker: Irwin
a15a1422253.text: Hold there, and I'll get the BSLSS bag ( 159k ) and all our...

a15a1422253.speaker: Scott
a15a1422253.text: Yeah, do that.

a15a1422253.speaker: Irwin
a15a1422253.text: ...gear. (Pause)

a15a1422253.speaker: Scott
a15a1422253.text: Okay, Houston. I'm out on the first rung of the ladder, and we'll take care of the jettison procedures here.

a15a1422253.speaker: Allen
a15a1422253.text: Okay, Dave. According to our calculations, here, you'll just about fill Hadley Rille with water (collected from behind the engine cover).

a15a1422253.speaker: Scott
a15a1422253.text: (Laughs) Yes, sorry to say. (Pause) Okay. That's...That a boy. Good. (Pause) Okay; one (water-filled LiOH) can's down. (Pause) [The timing in this sequence indicates that as Jim pushes the LiOH canisters and other articles out through the hatch, Dave takes them and drops them over the railing, probably on the right (south) side to avoid hitting the MESA.]

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1422537csm.text: As I look at the map, Al, it looks to me like you're going smack over Tsiolkovsky every rev now. How is it looking to you?

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1422537csm.text: That's just about right, Karl. Coming right over the middle of it.

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1422537csm.text: That's all right, Jim. Just like the last one. That a...Oop. Little...Push with your foot? That's good. I got it. Okay. Canister going down. (Pause) Okay; toss it right here. That a boy. (Pause) Okay, the other can is down. Okay, a Jett bag. I mean, the BSLSS bag.

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1422537csm.text: That must be a beautiful sight. Hey, I was sort of fascinated by the fact that, on your first couple of revs, you noted that you could really see the peaks sticking up - the central peak before you could see the rim. Is that really true?

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1422537csm.text: Yeah. (Long Pause)

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1422537csm.text: Okay.

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1422537csm.text: Just a minute...

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1422537csm.text: You dropped it. Oh! I've got it. (Pause) Okay; it's down. And if you can hand me the ETB.

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1422537csm.text: Stand by. (Long Pause) [The ETB contains the cameras and, consequently, Dave will carry it down by hand.]

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1422537csm.text: Easy does it; that's it.

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1422537csm.text: Got her?

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1422537csm.text: Hey, that would be great to get pictures of that. I don't know when you were scheduled to look at that - that landslide on the northwest corner of it, but are you seeing anything of that area?

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1422537csm.text: Yeah.

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1422537csm.text: Good. (Pause) 142:27:19 Scott: Okay, down the ladder to the plains of Hadley. (Long Pause) By golly. Just like we left it yesterday.

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1422537csm.text: Absolutely, I look at it every time I go by and there's just - there's no question in my mind at all that it is a - that it is a - rock avalanche. It - it does have some interesting qualities about it, though. And it's a little bit hard for me to decipher right now, but it seems like the density of crater impacts in that slide is - is greater than in the surrounding terrain, even though the slide had to be emplaced on top of the surrounding terrain. Maybe it's just that the craters are - are fresher in that - fresher looking in that particular material. But no question about the lineaments bei

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1422537csm.text: Jim, this is Houston with a request.

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1422537csm.text: (To Dave) Good. (To Joe) Go ahead, Joe.

a15_1422537csm.text: Roger, Jim. We're seeing some excursions in your Delta-P (pressure difference on) the Glycol Pump 1. We'd like for you to pull the Auto Transfer circuit breaker on that Glycol Pump, and select Pump number 2. Over.

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1422537csm.text: Okay, stand by. Okay, I'm pulling Auto Transfer now; and I'm selecting Pump 2. Is that affirm?

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1422537csm.text: Roger. That sounds interesting. [Pause.]

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1422537csm.text: That's affirm; thank you. (Long Pause) 142:29:05 Scott: (To himself) Okay. Pick up the pallet. (Long Pause) Oh, boy; is that easy and fixed. My! They will not do a pallet transfer during EVA-3.]

a15_1422537csm.text: Guess I'd add one other comment to that. So far, I haven't been able to locate the other one. [Pause.]

a15_1422537csm.text: So far, I haven't been able to locate Alvin.

a15_1422537csm.text: Pins is green, yeah.

a15_1422537csm.text: Well, tell him not to worry. I'm sure it's there and I'll - I've just got to get a little bit further south around the edge of the crater.

a15_1422537csm.text: Sounds good.

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1422537csm.text: Okay. Hey, when you can get the Flight Plan and a pencil, I've got a - a few more updates to finish up on this rev. [Pause.]

a15_1422537csm.text: Don't have to put an LiOH (canister for the ECS) in it. So, I guess it makes it little easier. [Jim loaded an ECS LiOH canister in Pallet No. 1 at about 120:52:24 during the early stages of EVA-1.]

a15_1422537csm.text: Just so there's plenty of food in it, Dave.

a15_1422537csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1422537csm.text: Yeah, that's a good idea. (Long Pause) [At some point, possibly here, Dave carries the pallet up the ladder to Jim. a15a1423239.text: Okay, I understand. At 151:10 you want that to read "Stereo Exposure, Normal;" and at 151:15, delete that line.

a15a1423239.text: Okay.

a15a1423239.speaker: Irwin
a15a1423239.text: Dave, if you are clear, I'm going to pitch the pallet out.

a15a1423239.speaker: Scott
a15a1423239.text: I'm clear, Jim. (Pause)

a15a1423239.speaker: Irwin
a15a1423239.text: And, Joe, I'm in a position to get out. Let me know what the final configuration is on the glycol pumps.

a15a1423239.speaker: Allen
a15a1423239.text: Jim, the best I can do for you right now is ask you to stand by one minute. We're going to make a final decision.

a15a1423239.speaker: Irwin
a15a1423239.text: Okay. (Long Pause)

a15a1423239.text: And, Dave, as you might guess, when Jim comes out, you can delete that step to deploy his antenna.

a15a1423239.speaker: Scott
a15a1423239.text: Yes, sir. Will do.

a15a1423239.speaker: Allen
a15a1423239.text: I have a very keen sense of the obvious.

a15a1423239.speaker: Scott
a15a1423239.text: No, that's a good reminder, Joe.

a15a1423239.speaker: Irwin
a15a1423239.text: Don't worry; I wouldn't let him do it, Joe.

a15a1423239.text: Shows you're thinking.

a15a1423239.speaker: Irwin
a15a1423239.text: But I sure would...(Stops to listen to Allen) Time's a wasting, Joe. (Pause) You're going to get way ahead of me, Dave.

a15_1423529csm.text: Endeavour, this is Houston. They have some data on that new DAP configuration, with the new weights. I guess we're not sure we want to stick with it, and at this time we'd like you to go back to the normal DAP load with the normal weight.

a15_1423529csm.text: It's alright. [Scott - "He's up there waiting for them to tell him on the glycol pumps. And he knows that our tasks are sequenced. We're working in parallel. So, he's saying I'm going to get way ahead of him, 'cause I'm doing my tasks and he should be doing his. He's standing up there, knowing he's falling behind and waiting for them to tell him about the glycol pumps, and wanting to get going."] [Jones - "Not only is it putting him a couple of minutes behind but, at some point, it's going to put you a couple of minutes behind."]

a15_1423529csm.text: Okay, Jim, requesting you go back...

a15_1423529csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1423529csm.text: Okay, going back to Pump 1.

a15_1423529csm.text: Okay, select Pump 1, Jim, and then close the...

And, as a young fighter pilot, you learn 'alpha, bravo, charlie, delta, echo.'"] [Jones - "And there are a couple of instances where people got playful and switched over to other systems. a15_1423529csm.text: And, Dave, as you climb on the Rover, we'll want all the meter readings before you start pushing in circuit breakers, please. And I'll remind you.

a15_1423529csm.text: Okay. (Long Pause)

Of course, for any spacecraft orientation, there was shadow of the plus-

a15_1423529csm.speaker: Scott

a15_1423529csm.text: Roger. [Dave is at 0:34 in his checklist. The EVA started at 142:14:44 and, therefore, Dave is actually about 7 minutes ahead of the timeline. In support of this conclusion, note that Jim is at about 0:31 in his checklist and, despite the delay caused by the glycol pump, he is also ahead of the timeline.]

a15_1424507csm.text: Roger. (Long Pause)
