a15_2764811.text: Well, I had - had the log out here, and I took a look at it, and at last count last night, we were 2,631 on Hasselblad pictures, total.

a15_2765106.speaker: Parker
a15_2765106.text: Roger, Dave. The interest in the mags was in reference to the UV - the mags for the UV photography tomorrow. So the interest was in the number of frames remaining on magazine Mike and magazine Papa, try - trying to determine which of those would be usable for tomorrow's UV photography.

a15_2765106.speaker: Scott
a15_2765106.text: Okay. I think we've got that log in the Flight Plan. Stand by 'til Al finishes his P23s, and we'll take a look.

a15_2765106.speaker: Scott
a15_2765106.text: [I] think we'll use a mag that has some film in it.

a15_2765106.speaker: Scott
a15_2765106.text: I said, at - at any rate, we'll use a mag that has some film in it tomorrow.

a15_2765706.speaker: Parker
a15_2765706.text: Apollo 15, Houston. Requesting Gamma-ray Gain Step, Shield, Off, now, please.

a15_2765706.speaker: Parker
a15_2765706.text: That was a good mark, Al. [Pause.]

a15_2765706.speaker: Worden
a15_2765706.text: Yeah, and it didn't update the state vector very much.

a15_2765706.speaker: Mission Control
a15_2765706.text: This is Apollo Control at 277 hours, 7 minutes. Al Worden is presently completing a series of star sightings - midcourse navigation exercise, using program 23 in the onboard computer. This will be the last major activity before the crew begins it's 9-hour rest period. After completing this, they'll go through the presleep checklist, get the systems set up for their sleep period and put the spacecraft in its Passive Thermal Control attitude, rotating at about the rate of 4 revolutions per hour. Apollo 15, at this time, is 89,626 nautical miles [165,987 km] from the Earth. The spacecraft velocit

a15_2770728.speaker: Parker
a15_2770728.text: Apollo 15, Houston.

a15_2770728.speaker: Worden
a15_2770728.text: Go ahead.

a15_2770728.speaker: Parker
a15_2770728.text: Roger. Congratulations, Al. You've just been voted to receive a second Vasco da Gama award for that. We were afraid you were going to do them all the way through the rest period.

a15_2770728.speaker: Worden
a15_2770728.text: Well, they're fun enough. I wouldn't mind.

a15_2770728.speaker: Irwin
a15_2770728.text: So were we.

a15_2770728.speaker: Parker
a15_2770728.text: [Laughter.] Okay; and...

a15_2770728.speaker: Worden
a15_2770728.text: It wouldn't have taken nearly so long if you hadn't wanted five marks per each star. [Pause.]

a15_2770728.speaker: Parker
a15_2770728.text: Rog, Al. I'll tell you about that some time. And, 15, we're configured for the E-mod dump, if you fellows want to give it to us.

a15_2770728.speaker: Scott
a15_2770728.text: Okay, it[the E-mod dump]'s coming. Does the bio data look any better?

a15_2770728.speaker: Parker
a15_2770728.text: Rog. Yes, it does.

a15_2770728.speaker: Scott
a15_2770728.text: Okay.

a15_2770728.speaker: Parker
a15_2770728.text: And, as you get ready for PTC, we'd like to do the PTC at 0.42 [degrees per second] there again tonight as last night, although it's changing the Noun 79 value there at 277:14. [Pause.]

a15_2770728.speaker: Worden
a15_2770728.text: Rog, Bob. I guess we use that as standard procedure now, the 4200.

a15_2770728.speaker: Parker
a15_2770728.text: Rog. You don't have to do it tomorrow night that way, though.

a15_2770728.speaker: Scott
a15_2770728.text: Okay. Use a different number tomorrow night.

a15_2770728.speaker: Parker
a15_2770728.text: And, Apollo 15, be advised that tomorrow when you're taking your P23 marks, five marks on the cal[ibraton star] and then 3 marks on the [other] stars with the P23 itself will be sufficient.

a15_2770728.speaker: Worden
a15_2770728.text: Okay, understand. 5 marks on the cal and 3 on each star.

a15_2770728.speaker: Parker
a15_2770728.text: Roger. Roger. [Long pause.]

a15_2770728.speaker: Scott
a15_2770728.text: Hey, Houston, 15. We've got the presleep checklist ready, too.

a15_2770728.speaker: Parker
a15_2770728.text: Roger. We're standing by.

a15_2770728.speaker: Scott
a15_2770728.text: The crew's all ready for bed, no medications, and the onboard read-out: Battery C, 37; Pyro Bat A, 37.1; B, 37.1; RCS A, 55; B, 50; C, 48; D, 52. And I guess everything else is done. You've got your E-memory dump, and we're ready to power down as soon as we get the PTC going.

a15_2770728.speaker: Parker
a15_2770728.text: Roger, Dave. As far as we're concerned, we're all finished also. We will not be uplinking a state vector to you. We might have to do that sometime just for practice, but so far we haven't needed to uplink one to you. You guys are doing pretty super on those P23s.

a15_2770728.speaker: Scott
a15_2770728.text: Compensating errors. [Pause.]

a15_2770728.speaker: Parker
a15_2770728.text: I can't believe that was a unanimous vote, Dave. [Pause.]

a15_2770728.speaker: Scott
a15_2770728.text: No, it was only two to one.

a15_2770728.speaker: [Unintentional key] MCC
a15_2770728.text: Okay, G&C. Let me know when he's in his rate amp.

a15_2772852.speaker: Parker
a15_2772852.text: Apollo 15, Houston. You're Go to start to spinup for PTC.

a15_2772852.speaker: Parker
a15_2772852.text: And, Apollo 15, we'd like you to check that the Potable Tank Inlet valve is open, please.

a15_2772852.speaker: Worden
a15_2772852.text: Roger; understand. Potable Tank Inlet valve, open. [Long pause.]

a15_2772852.speaker: Scott
a15_2772852.text: Okay. Listen, potable tank inlet valve is open and has been the whole flight. What prompted the question?

a15_2772852.speaker: Parker
a15_2772852.text: 15, we saw a drop in the potable at the same time that the waste tank was staying stable, and we were - just concerned that it might have gotten out of configuration. We certainly expected it to be open; we just wanted to check it before you went to sleep, so we didn't have to wake you up.

a15_2772852.speaker: Scott
a15_2772852.text: Okay. Understand. Yeah - we're reading potable at 90 percent.

a15_2774352.speaker: Parker
a15_2774352.text: Apollo 15, Houston. No need to acknowledge, but we'd like to put the DSKY to sleep before you guys go to sleep.

a15_2774352.speaker: Mission Control
a15_2774352.text: This is Apollo Control at 278 hours, 2 minutes. Flight Surgeon reports that Dave Scott, the only crewman on whom we have biomedical data tonight, appears to be nearing sleep, at least beginning to drop off, and we expect that he'll be sleeping shortly. During this sleep period, we don't expect any further conversation with the crew. The Passive Thermal Control mode appears to be stable. We're watching the attitude excursions, the movements that the spacecraft is making about its axis and it appears to be quite stable. Looks as if it will hold throughout the sleep period. At the present time, A

a15_2774352.speaker: Mission Control
a15_2774352.text: This is Apollo Control at 278 hours, 36 minutes. At the present time, we're replaying the video and audio from the inflight press conference today. This can be seen in the MSC News Center.

a15_2774352.speaker: Mission Control
a15_2774352.text: This is Apollo Control at 281 hours, 27 minutes. The crew of Apollo 15 asleep at this time. Five hours and two minutes remaining until they will be wakened for preparations for entry and Earth-landing later this afternoon. Splashdown clock showing 13 hours, 43 minutes until splash. The spacecraft, at this time, is 74,650 nautical miles [138,252 kilometres] out in space approaching Earth. Velocity continuing to increase; now showing 6,435 feet per second [1,961 metres per second]. Current vector on the spacecraft still showing entry angle and Entry Interface at minus 6.5 degrees.
